# Brake Check Procedure for New Volunteers

Read this whole page before you touch a customer bike. If any step fails, do not return the bike to the customer. Tag it and tell the shop lead.

## Before you start

1. Stand the bike upright in the work stand, or flip it onto its wheels on a flat floor.
2. Confirm you know which brake type the bike has. Rim brakes clamp the wheel rim. Disc brakes have a metal rotor bolted to the hub and a caliper that clamps the rotor.
3. Wipe your hands. Oil on a pad or rotor will cause the brake to fail.

## Part A: Rim brakes

### A1. Brake pads
- Look at the pad rubber. Replace the pad if the rubber is worn down to the wear groove or indicator line.
- Replace the pad if the rubber is cracked, hardened, glazed (shiny), or has a metal piece exposed.
- Check that the pad is seated firmly in its holder and the holder bolt is tight.

### A2. Pad alignment
- The pad should contact the braking surface of the rim, not the tire and not the rim's upper edge.
- The front edge of the pad should sit slightly closer to the rim than the back edge (toe-in). A small amount of toe-in makes the pad squeal less and grip better.
- Squeeze the lever and check that both pads touch the rim at the same time.

### A3. Rim braking surface
- Look at the rim sidewall where the pads contact it. Replace the rim if the wear indicator groove is gone or the sidewall is bulging, cracked, or flaking.
- Spin the wheel. A side-to-side wobble that rubs the pads means the wheel needs truing. Send it to the lead.

### A4. Cable and lever
- Squeeze the lever. It should stop well before the bar and feel firm. Spongy or slow return means the cable needs adjusting or the return spring is weak.
- Check the cable for fraying, kinks, or rust. Replace a damaged cable.
- Check that the quick release or cable clamp bolt is fully closed.
- Check that the brake arm springs pull the arms back open when the lever is released.

### A5. Brake bolts
- Check that the brake mounting bolt is tight and the brake does not move when you push it.

## Part B: Disc brakes

### B1. Brake pads
- Look at each pad through the caliper opening. Replace the pad when the friction material is less than about 1 mm thick, or when it is at the wear line on the pad.
- Check for glazed, cracked, or contaminated pads. Replace any pad that is contaminated with oil or grease.
- Check that the pad retaining pin or clip is in place.

### B2. Rotor
- Look for scoring or deep grooves on the braking surface. Light marks are normal. Deep grooves mean the rotor should be replaced.
- Check for cracks, especially around the bolt holes. Replace a cracked rotor.
- Spin the wheel and watch the rotor edge. A wobble or a rub means the rotor is bent. Send the wheel to the lead.
- Check the thickness marking stamped on the rotor against the minimum thickness. Replace the rotor if it is at or below the minimum.

### B3. Rotor bolts and caliper mount
- Check that all rotor bolts are tight. Use the torque spec printed on the rotor or the manufacturer's manual.
- Check that the caliper mounting bolts are tight.

### B4. Caliper and cable (mechanical disc)
- Squeeze the lever. It should stop well before the bar and feel firm.
- Check the cable for fraying, kinks, or rust.
- Check that the caliper centers over the rotor with no rubbing when the lever is released. If it rubs, adjust the caliper centering.

### B5. Hydraulic brakes
- Check the lever feel. The lever should feel firm and bite early. A soft or spongy lever means air in the line or a leak. Tag the bike and send it to the lead for a bleed.
- Look for fluid leaks at the lever, hose fittings, and caliper.
- Check the fluid reservoir level. Do not top up with a different fluid type.

## Part C: Final test (both brake types)

1. Spin the wheel with the brakes off. Confirm the wheel spins freely with no rubbing.
2. Squeeze each brake lever. Confirm the brake grabs the wheel, or the rotor, evenly.
3. Check the quick release or thru axle is fully closed.
4. Ride the bike slowly in a clear area. Brake at low speed, then at a higher speed. Confirm the bike stops straight with no pulling to one side.
5. Check the lever does not go to the bar during a hard stop.

## When to stop and tag the bike

Tag the bike and tell the shop lead if you see any of these:
- A pad, rotor, or rim is worn past its limit, cracked, or bent.
- A brake rubs when released or does not stop the bike.
- A bolt will not tighten, or a bolt looks stripped or cracked.
- Oil or fluid on a pad or rotor.
- A hydraulic lever feels spongy or leaks.
- Any step in this procedure that you are not sure about.

Do not guess. A brake that is not sure to work is not safe to return to a customer.

# Torque Wrench Guide for Bicycles

## What a torque wrench is for

A torque wrench measures how hard a bolt is tightened. Most bike bolts are small, and the right tightness sits in a narrow range. A feel-based tightening can miss that range by a wide margin, so a torque wrench gives a repeatable number in newton metres (Nm).

Too little torque lets parts loosen, creak, slip, or come apart under load. Too much torque can strip threads, crush or crack carbon fibre, gall aluminium, deform clamps, or make a part very hard to remove later. Carbon parts are the main reason to use a torque wrench, because carbon can fail without warning when overtightened.

Torque wrenches are most useful on parts that bear load or clamp a component: stems, handlebars, seatposts, brake and drivetrain mounts, cranks, and wheel axles.

## Practical rules

- Always check the value printed on the part first. Manufacturer values override the general figures below.
- Use a bit that fits the bolt head fully. A loose fit rounds the head.
- Apply a thin film of the correct lubricant only where the manufacturer specifies it. Some threads, such as carbon clamp bolts, need grease or none at all. Lubricant changes the torque reading, so follow the spec for that condition.
- Tighten in a cross pattern on multi-bolt parts, such as stem faceplates and rotor bolts.
- Use a click-type or beam-type wrench that is calibrated. Set a click wrench back to its lowest setting after use so the spring is not stressed.
- Do not use a torque wrench to loosen bolts. Breaking a bolt loose with a torque wrench can damage the tool.

## Common torque values

These are typical figures for many bikes. They are not universal. Always confirm against the manufacturer marking or manual.

| Component | Typical torque | Reason for this value |
|---|---|---|
| Stem faceplate bolts | 5 to 6 Nm | Clamps the bar. Too tight can crack carbon bars or deform the steerer. |
| Stem to steerer expander bolt | 5 to 6 Nm | Expands the steerer plug to hold the stem. Too tight can crack the fork steerer. |
| Handlebar clamp bolts (stem) | 5 to 6 Nm | Holds the bar without crushing it. Carbon bars often specify a lower value. |
| Seatpost clamp bolt | 5 to 6 Nm | Holds the post. Carbon posts often need a specified value and grease check. |
| Saddle rail clamp bolts | 5 to 7 Nm | Holds the saddle rails. Too loose lets the saddle rotate. |
| Brake lever clamp bolts | 5 to 6 Nm | Holds the lever to the bar. Overtightening can crack carbon bars. |
| Brake caliper mount bolts | 6 to 8 Nm | Secures the caliper to the frame or fork. Loose mounts cause rubbing and poor braking. |
| Disc rotor bolts (6 bolt) | 2.5 to 4 Nm | Holds the rotor to the hub. Overtightening warps rotors and can crack alloy hubs. |
| Centerlock rotor lockring | About 40 Nm (check spec) | Locks the rotor on a splined carrier. Requires a dedicated lockring tool. |
| Front derailleur clamp bolt | 5 to 6 Nm | Clamps the derailleur to the seat tube. Overtightening can crush the tube. |
| Rear derailleur mounting bolt | 8 to 10 Nm | Holds the derailleur to the hanger. Loose bolts shift the derailleur. |
| Shifter and brake lever bolts | 5 to 6 Nm | Holds controls in place. Too loose lets them rotate. |
| Chainring bolts | 8 to 12 Nm | Secures rings to the crank spider. Loose rings wear and can detach. |
| Crank arm bolt (Hollowtech or similar) | 35 to 50 Nm | Holds the crank to the spindle. Loose cranks damage the spindle and can come off. |
| Pedals into crank | 30 to 35 Nm | Holds the pedal in the crank. Under-tightening can strip the crank threads. |
| Bottom bracket | 35 to 50 Nm (varies widely) | Holds the cups in the frame. Specs differ by bracket type. |
| Cassette lockring | 30 to 50 Nm | Holds the cassette on the freehub. Loose cassettes click and wear. |
| Thru axle (12 mm rear or front) | 15 to 20 Nm | Clamps the wheel in the dropouts. Loose axles allow the wheel to shift. |
| Water bottle cage bolts | 1 to 2 Nm | Holds the cage without crushing the frame. Carbon frames need the low end. |
| Rack and fender mounts | Varies by mount | Follow the rack or frame manual. Eyelets and bolts differ widely. |

Quick release skewers are set by lever tension, not a torque wrench. Nipples are not torqued; true wheels by tension and alignment.

## Carbon and special cases

- Carbon parts: use the lowest value the manufacturer allows, and never exceed the printed maximum.
- Aluminium threads gall easily. A small amount of anti-seize may be specified on steel bolts into aluminium parts.
- Bolts into carbon frames or forks usually need a specified torque and grease. Do not guess.

# Week-Long Bike Tour Packing Guide

Assumptions: self-supported tour, 7 days, mixed weather, a mix of hotels and campsites, roughly 50 to 70 miles riding per day. Adjust the clothing and tools if your route differs.

## Bike and safety (check before the trip)
- Tires: inspect for cuts and wear. Replace any tire with a worn tread or sidewall damage. Reason: a failed tire on day 3 with no spare can end the tour.
- Spare tubes: carry 2 tubes in the correct size. Reason: one flat is common, two covers a second flat before a shop visit.
- Tire levers (2 to 3) and a patch kit. Reason: levers free a tire from the rim, and patches fix small punctures.
- Mini pump or CO2 inflator with spare cartridges. Reason: a pump is reusable, while CO2 is fast but gives you only a few fills.
- Multitool with hex keys, chain tool, and a spoke wrench. Reason: covers most roadside adjustments.
- Chain lube and a rag. Reason: a dry chain wears fast and squeaks on long days.
- Brake pads: check thickness. Reason: 7 days of descents wear pads quickly.
- Helmet, front and rear lights, and a bell. Reason: lights keep you visible in tunnels, fog and early or late riding.
- Bike mirror (optional). Reason: lets you watch traffic without turning your head.
- Bottle cages and at least 2 water bottles. Reason: heat and climbs raise water needs.
- Saddle bag or frame bag for the tools above. Reason: keeps repair kit reachable on the road.

## Clothing
- Cycling shorts: 2 pairs. Reason: one can dry while you ride in the other.
- Riding jerseys: 3 to 4. Reason: rotate to limit odor, and moisture wicking keeps you cooler.
- Base layer: 1 long sleeve. Reason: warmth for cold mornings and descents.
- Lightweight rain jacket and rain pants or leg covers. Reason: wet weather is the main risk to comfort and body heat.
- Arm warmers or a light fleece. Reason: cover the temperature swing from morning to afternoon.
- Gloves: full-finger riding gloves. Reason: protects hands in a fall and on long descents.
- Socks: 4 to 5 pairs of cycling socks. Reason: fresh socks prevent blisters and foot problems.
- Casual clothes: 1 set for evenings. Reason: lets you change out of cycling kit at hotels and cafes.
- Sleep clothes: 1 set. Reason: clean clothing helps recovery.
- Sun hat or cap under the helmet, plus sunglasses. Reason: protects face and eyes from long exposure.
- Underwear: 6 to 7 sets. Reason: one set per day.

## Health and personal care
- Chamois cream. Reason: reduces saddle sores and chafing on long days.
- Sunscreen SPF 30 or higher, lip balm with SPF. Reason: sun exposure adds up over 50 to 70 miles a day.
- Insect repellent. Reason: needed on rural routes and near water.
- First aid kit: bandages, blister pads, pain relievers, antihistamine, antiseptic wipes, personal prescriptions. Reason: most tour injuries are blisters, scrapes and minor illness.
- Toiletries: travel size, quick-dry towel. Reason: small and fast to dry.
- Hand sanitizer and wet wipes. Reason: useful when water or soap is scarce.

## Nutrition and hydration
- Energy bars and gels. Reason: quick fuel for climbs and long gaps between towns.
- Electrolyte tablets. Reason: replaces salt lost in sweat on hot days.
- Reusable water bottles. Reason: avoids buying single-use bottles.

## Navigation and electronics
- Phone with downloaded offline maps and route file. Reason: signal can drop in rural areas.
- Phone mount for the handlebars. Reason: keeps navigation visible without stopping.
- Power bank (10,000 mAh or larger) and short charging cable. Reason: a phone can drain by midday with mapping and camera use.
- Wall charger and adapter for your destination. Reason: keeps devices charged at hotels.
- Headphones (optional). Reason: music can help pacing, but do not block traffic sounds.

## Documents and money
- Printed copy of the itinerary, bookings, and emergency contacts. Reason: works if the phone fails.
- ID, insurance card, and emergency contact details. Reason: needed for care if something goes wrong.
- Cash and a card. Reason: some rural stops do not accept cards.

## Packing and carrying
- Panniers or a rack-mounted bag system, or a frame bag and seat bag. Reason: balanced weight keeps handling stable.
- Dry bags or packing cubes. Reason: keep clothes dry in rain and simple to find.
- Keep heavy items low and near the center. Reason: low weight improves stability on descents and in wind.
- Weigh the loaded bag before the trip. Reason: heavy loads strain the rack and wheels.

## Before you leave
- Test-ride the loaded bike for 20 minutes. Reason: finds balance or rack problems early.
- Service the drivetrain and brakes. Reason: mechanical failure is the most common reason for a lost day.
- Confirm bike box or bike travel rules with your airline if flying. Reason: airline rules for bikes vary.

# Brake Check Procedure for New Volunteers

Stop and tag any bike that fails a step. Put a DO NOT RIDE tag on the handlebars and tell the lead mechanic. Never ride a bike with a brake you have doubts about.

## Before you start

1. Wear eye protection if you will use compressed air or solvent.
2. Stand the bike in the work stand or lean it on a wall with the wheels off the floor.
3. Check the quick release levers or axle nuts first. Both wheels must be fully seated and tight.

## Part A: Rim brakes

Rim brakes squeeze the wheel rim. The pads must touch the rim braking surface, never the tire.

1. Pad wear. Look for the wear indicator groove on each pad. If the groove is gone, or the pad is cracked, hard, glazed, or oily, replace the pad.
2. Pad contact. Squeeze the lever and check that the pad sits flat on the rim braking track. Pads must not touch the tire sidewall or the rim edge.
3. Pad toe-in. The front edge of each pad should touch the rim slightly before the back edge. Set a gap of about 1 mm at the front edge.
4. Centering. Spin the wheel. Both pads should sit the same distance from the rim. Adjust the centering screw on the caliper if one side rubs.
5. Caliper bolt. Check that the caliper mounting bolt is tight and the caliper does not rock.
6. Cable. Squeeze the lever. The pads should close evenly and the lever should stop with a firm feel. Check that the cable pinch bolt is tight and the cable is not frayed.
7. Rim wear. Look at the rim braking track. Stop and tag the wheel if you see a deep groove, a bulge, a crack, or a hole in the rim wall.
8. Lever feel. Squeeze the lever hard. It should not touch the handlebar grip. If it does, adjust cable tension.
9. Final test. Spin the wheel, then squeeze each lever. The wheel should slow evenly and stop. There should be no rubbing, squeal from a loose pad, or grabbing.

## Part B: Disc brakes

Disc brakes squeeze a rotor on the hub. Rotors get hot and can burn your fingers after riding, so let them cool first.

1. Rotor condition. Look for bends, cracks, deep grooves, or blue discoloration. Stop and tag the wheel if the rotor is bent or cracked.
2. Rotor bolts. Check that all rotor bolts are tight in a star pattern.
3. Rotor clean. Wipe the rotor with disc brake cleaner on a clean rag. Never spray lubricant or any oil on a rotor or pad.
4. Pad condition. Check the friction material thickness. Replace the pads if they are worn to the wear line, or if they are oily, glazed, or cracked. Do not touch the pad friction surface with bare fingers.
5. Caliper mount. Check that both caliper mounting bolts are tight. The caliper should not rock.
6. Rotor alignment. Spin the wheel. The rotor should run through the caliper without touching either pad. Listen for a steady rub. Adjust the caliper position if the rotor rubs.
7. Hydraulic brakes. Squeeze the lever. It should feel firm and not spongy. Check the hose and fittings for leaks. If the lever feels soft or spongy, do not ride. Tag the bike and tell the lead mechanic, because the system likely needs bleeding.
8. Mechanical brakes. Squeeze the lever. Cable tension should stop the wheel with a firm lever feel. Check that the cable pinch bolt is tight.
9. Final test. Spin the wheel, then squeeze each lever. The wheel should slow and stop without a rub, squeal, or grabbing.

## Sign off

Only return a bike to the floor when both wheels pass the final test and every step above is done. Write the bike tag with your initials and the date. If any step failed, leave the DO NOT RIDE tag on and tell the lead mechanic.

# Week-Long Bike Tour Packing Guide

Assumptions: self-supported tour, about 7 days, 40 to 70 miles per day, camping or hotels, one rear pannier setup, mixed weather. Adjust quantities to your trip.

## 1. Bike and safety (carry or check)
- Helmet: required for most rides and protects against the most common serious injury.
- Lights: front and rear, plus spare batteries or a charger. Tours include dusk and tunnel riding.
- Lock: a U-lock or cable lock for stops at cafes and campsites.
- Bike multi-tool with chain tool, spoke wrench, hex keys, and tire levers: most roadside problems need one of these.
- Two spare tubes (or one tube plus a patch kit): flats are the most common breakdown on tour.
- Mini pump or CO2 inflator with spare cartridge: a pump that fits the tube valve type (Presta or Schrader).
- Spare chain links and a quick link: a broken chain without a fix ends the day.
- Brake pads, cable, and derailleur hanger: carry a spare if your bike is old or the route is remote.
- Bike bag or box if flying: protects the frame and makes the check-in process easier.

## 2. Clothing (layered for changing weather)
- Cycling shorts: 2 pairs, so one can dry while the other is worn. Padding reduces saddle soreness.
- Riding jerseys: 3 short sleeve, quick drying. Cotton holds sweat and stays wet.
- Base layer (long sleeve): 1, for cold mornings and rain.
- Lightweight rain jacket: waterproof and breathable, for the weather you cannot avoid.
- Arm warmers or a light wind vest: 1, for cool descents.
- Sleep or casual clothes: 1 set, for evenings off the bike.
- Underwear and socks: 6 pairs of each, enough for 7 days with one wash.
- Cycling gloves: 1 pair, padded, for road vibration and falls.
- Sun gloves or sunglasses: sun and glare add to fatigue.
- Shoes: cycling shoes or sturdy riding shoes, plus sandals for evenings to give your feet a change.

## 3. Camping and sleep (if camping)
- Tent, sleeping bag rated for the lowest expected temperature, and sleeping pad: the pad is the most important insulator.
- Lightweight camp towel and toiletry kit: keeps hygiene simple between showers.

## 4. Toiletries and health
- Sunscreen (SPF 30 or higher), lip balm with SPF.
- Chamois cream: reduces friction and saddle sores on long days.
- Basic first aid kit: adhesive strips, antiseptic, blister pads, pain relief, personal prescriptions.
- Insect repellent: needed in wooded or wet areas.
- Electrolyte tablets and a refillable water bottle set (2 bottles minimum): dehydration reduces pace and judgment.

## 5. Electronics and documents
- Phone with offline maps downloaded, plus a cable and charger. Offline maps keep you on route without signal.
- Power bank (10,000 mAh or more): one full charge is usually not enough for a full day of navigation.
- Head torch or headlamp: for camp and early departures.
- Passport or ID, travel insurance card, emergency contacts, and a printed copy of the route and bookings. Paper backups work when phones die.
- Cash in small notes: some rural stops do not take cards.

## 6. Packing layout
- Heavy items low and centered in the panniers to keep the bike stable.
- Keep the rain jacket, first aid kit, and phone reachable without unpacking.
- Use dry bags or a rain cover for all gear. Wet sleeping gear is hard to recover.
- Target a total load of about 10 to 15 kg (22 to 33 lb) in bags, excluding the bike. Heavier loads slow climbing and braking.

## 7. Before you fly
- Remove pedals and turn the handlebars parallel to the frame, then wrap the bike box or bag with padding.
- Deflate tires slightly if the carrier requires it.
- Check airline rules for bike fees and size limits. Confirm the tool kit is packed in checked luggage, since many airlines ban multi-tools and CO2 cartridges in carry-on bags.
- Take a photo of the packed bike and your bag contents for insurance claims.

## 8. Before day one
- Test ride the loaded bike for 20 to 30 minutes to check handling and gear range.
- Check tire pressure, brake pad wear, and chain condition.
- Confirm the route, daily distances, and water stops.

## Reasoning summary
The list favors spares for failures that stop a rider (flats, chains, brakes), layers for shifting weather, and offline navigation because a tour spends long hours without signal. Weight is capped so the bike handles safely on climbs and descents.

# Roadside Tube Patch Guide

This guide walks through fixing a flat inner tube with a patch kit, step by step.

## What you need
- Patch kit (patches, sandpaper or scuffer, rubber cement or glue, chalk or a marker)
- Tire levers (two or three, plastic is fine)
- Pump (hand pump or CO2 inflator)
- Small bowl of water, or your cheek, for finding leaks
- A rag

Pull over somewhere safe. Turn the bike upside down or rest it on the saddle and handlebars.

- Rear wheel: shift the chain onto the smallest rear cog, then open the quick release lever or loosen the axle nuts. Lift the chain off the cog if needed, then pull the wheel out.
- Front wheel: open the quick release or loosen the axle nuts, then lift the wheel out.

## Step 3: Let the air out
Press the valve pin on the tire valve to release any remaining air. For a Presta valve (thin, with a small lock nut on top), unscrew the top nut first, then press the pin.

## Step 4: Remove the tire
1. Push one bead (tire edge) off the rim all the way around on one side, using your hands first.
2. Hook a tire lever under the bead, about 10 cm from the valve.
3. Pry the tire up and hook the lever onto a spoke so it stays in place.
4. Use a second lever about 5 cm further along to work the bead off the rim.
5. Pull the valve out of the rim hole, then work the tire off the rim.
6. Pull the tube out of the tire. Keep the tire in place if possible, to check it later.

## Step 5: Find the leak
1. Pump the tube up a little so it holds its shape.
2. Feel along the tube for air, or dip sections into water and watch for bubbles.
3. Mark the hole with chalk or a marker.
4. Check the tire inside for anything sharp (glass, thorns, wire). Remove it. Otherwise it will puncture the new tube.

## Step 6: Prepare the patch
1. Dry the area around the hole.
2. Scuff a patch-sized area around the hole with sandpaper, about 2 to 3 times the patch size. Remove the shiny surface.
3. Wipe away the dust.

## Step 7: Apply glue
1. Spread a thin, even layer of rubber cement over the scuffed area.
2. Wait until it is tacky, usually 1 to 3 minutes. It should not feel wet.

## Step 8: Attach the patch
1. Peel the foil off the patch. Do not touch the adhesive side with your fingers.
2. Place the patch centered over the hole.
3. Press hard for 30 seconds or more. Roll a tire lever or a bottle over it if you can.

## Step 9: Reinstall the tube
1. Put a little air in the tube so it takes shape.
2. Insert the valve into the rim hole first. Then tuck the tube inside the tire, keeping it flat with no twists.
3. Check the tire bead sits in the rim center channel all the way around.

## Step 10: Put the tire back on
1. Start at the valve and push the bead back onto the rim with your hands.
2. Work toward both sides. The last section is the hardest. Use a lever only if needed, and take care not to pinch the tube.
3. Push the tire all the way around, then check the tube is not caught under the bead.

## Step 11: Inflate
1. Inflate to the pressure printed on the tire sidewall, usually 80 to 130 psi for road tires. Less is fine for a roadside fix.
2. Watch the bead on both sides. It should be even all around.
3. Wait 1 to 2 minutes, then check pressure again.

1. Line the wheel up in the frame and seat it fully.
2. Rear wheel: put the chain back on the cog, make sure the wheel sits centered in the dropouts.
3. Close the quick release firmly. Tighten the axle nuts if you used them.
4. Spin the wheel and check it does not rub the brakes.

## Step 13: Check and ride
Squeeze the tire to make sure it is firm. Ride slowly for a short distance and check the tire again.

- Carry a spare tube. Swapping a tube is faster than patching on the road.
- Patching is best done at home. A roadside patch can fail later.
- If the hole is larger than the patch or on the sidewall, replace the tube.

# Roadside Tube Patch Guide

Safety first: pull fully off the road, keep the bike away from traffic, and wear gloves if you have them. Work slowly. Rushing causes pinched tubes and lost parts.

## What you need

- Tire levers (2 or 3, plastic is best)
- Patch kit (glue or self-adhesive patches, sandpaper or the scuffer in the kit)
- Spare tube or the old one if it is repairable
- Small pump (frame or mini pump)
- A bowl of water, or your hands and eyes, to find the leak
- Rag

## Step 1: Find the wheel

If the flat is on the back wheel, shift into the smallest rear gear first. This takes tension off the chain. Open the brake quick release lever on rim brakes if the tire is tight. Then undo the quick release skewer or wheel nuts and lift the wheel out.

## Step 2: Let out the air

Press the valve core in with a fingernail or the tip of a tool. Presta valves (thin, with a small lock nut on top) need the top nut loosened first. Push the valve core in until air hisses out.

## Step 3: Remove one side of the tire

1. Push the bead (tire edge) on the side opposite the valve into the center of the rim. This gives slack.
2. Hook the first tire lever under the bead, about 10 cm from the valve. Do not use a sharp tool.
3. Pry the lever up and hook it onto a spoke. Keep the hooked spoke area clear of the rest of the tire.
4. Use a second lever a hand width away and pry the bead over the rim. Repeat until one side is free.
5. Pull the tube out of the tire, starting at the valve.

## Step 4: Check the tire

Run your fingers slowly around the inside of the tire. Feel for glass, thorns, or wire. Remove anything you find. A sharp object left inside will puncture the new tube too.

## Step 5: Find the leak

1. Pump a little air into the tube so it is firm but not tight.
2. Hold it near your cheek or ear and turn it slowly. Feel or listen for air.
3. Or dip sections into water and look for bubbles.
4. Mark the hole with a pen or chalk.

If you cannot find the leak, use a spare tube. Mark the leak later at home.

## Step 6: Patch the tube (if you are using a patch kit)

1. Dry the tube and mark the leak area with a pen. Patch about 2 cm around the hole.
2. Scuff the area with sandpaper or the kit scuffer until the surface looks dull. This helps the glue stick.
3. Apply a thin layer of glue to the scuffed area. Wait until the glue is tacky, usually 1 to 2 minutes, and not wet.
4. Peel the foil off the patch. Press it firmly onto the glue for about 30 seconds. Hold down the edges.
5. Let the patch cure for the time on the kit, often 5 minutes or more. Do not inflate before the patch sets.

Self-adhesive patches: scuff, clean with the alcohol wipe if supplied, peel and press.

## Step 7: Put the tube back in the tire

1. Pump a small amount of air into the tube so it takes shape. This stops it from folding inside the tire.
2. Push the valve through the rim hole first.
3. Tuck the tube inside the tire evenly. Check that no part of the tube sticks out at the bead.
4. Push the tire bead back onto the rim, working from the valve in both directions. Use your thumbs first. Use a lever only at the last part, and take care not to pinch the tube.

## Step 8: Inflate

1. Pump the tire to the pressure printed on the sidewall. A small pump may need many strokes.
2. Check that the bead sits evenly on both sides of the rim. You should see a thin line of rim all around.
3. If the tire bulges or the tube shows at a bead, let the air out and start again.

## Step 9: Refit the wheel

Seat the wheel in the frame. Make sure it is centered between the brake pads or the chainstay and seatstay. Tighten the quick release or axle nuts firmly. Reconnect the brake, then spin the wheel to check that it does not rub.

## Common mistakes

- Pinched tube: a line of two small holes from the lever. Let the air out and reseat the tire more carefully.
- Valve at the wrong angle: the tube will bulge near the valve. Check that the tube sits square.
- Forgetting to tighten the wheel: the wheel can slip or come loose while you ride.

## After you get home

Find the leak with water. Clean and dry the tube. Check the tire carefully for the cause of the puncture.

# Roadside Tube Patch Guide

Safety first: pull fully off the road, keep the bike away from traffic, and wear gloves if you have them. Work slowly. Rushing causes pinched tubes and lost parts.

## What you need

- Tire levers (2 or 3, plastic is best)
- Patch kit (glue or self-adhesive patches, sandpaper or the scuffer in the kit)
- Spare tube or the old one if it is repairable
- Small pump (frame or mini pump)
- A bowl of water, or your hands and eyes, to find the leak
- Rag

## Step 1: Find the wheel

If the flat is on the back wheel, shift into the smallest rear gear first. This takes tension off the chain. Open the brake quick release lever on rim brakes if the tire is tight. Then undo the quick release skewer or wheel nuts and lift the wheel out.

## Step 2: Let out the air

Press the valve core in with a fingernail or the tip of a tool. Presta valves (thin, with a small lock nut on top) need the top nut loosened first. Push the valve core in until air hisses out.

## Step 3: Remove one side of the tire

1. Push the bead (tire edge) on the side opposite the valve into the center of the rim. This gives slack.
2. Hook the first tire lever under the bead, about 10 cm from the valve. Do not use a sharp tool.
3. Pry the lever up and hook it onto a spoke. Keep the hooked spoke area clear of the rest of the tire.
4. Use a second lever a hand width away and pry the bead over the rim. Repeat until one side is free.
5. Pull the tube out of the tire, starting at the valve.

## Step 4: Check the tire

Run your fingers slowly around the inside of the tire. Feel for glass, thorns, or wire. Remove anything you find. A sharp object left inside will puncture the new tube too.

## Step 5: Find the leak

1. Pump a little air into the tube so it is firm but not tight.
2. Hold it near your cheek or ear and turn it slowly. Feel or listen for air.
3. Or dip sections into water and look for bubbles.
4. Mark the hole with a pen or chalk.

If you cannot find the leak, use a spare tube. Mark the leak later at home.

## Step 6: Patch the tube (if you are using a patch kit)

1. Dry the tube and mark the leak area with a pen. Patch about 2 cm around the hole.
2. Scuff the area with sandpaper or the kit scuffer until the surface looks dull. This helps the glue stick.
3. Apply a thin layer of glue to the scuffed area. Wait until the glue is tacky, usually 1 to 2 minutes, and not wet.
4. Peel the foil off the patch. Press it firmly onto the glue for about 30 seconds. Hold down the edges.
5. Let the patch cure for the time on the kit, often 5 minutes or more. Do not inflate before the patch sets.

Self-adhesive patches: scuff, clean with the alcohol wipe if supplied, peel and press.

## Step 7: Put the tube back in the tire

1. Pump a small amount of air into the tube so it takes shape. This stops it from folding inside the tire.
2. Push the valve through the rim hole first.
3. Tuck the tube inside the tire evenly. Check that no part of the tube sticks out at the bead.
4. Push the tire bead back onto the rim, working from the valve in both directions. Use your thumbs first. Use a lever only at the last part, and take care not to pinch the tube.

## Step 8: Inflate

1. Pump the tire to the pressure printed on the sidewall. A small pump may need many strokes.
2. Check that the bead sits evenly on both sides of the rim. You should see a thin line of rim all around.
3. If the tire bulges or the tube shows at a bead, let the air out and start again.

## Step 9: Refit the wheel

Seat the wheel in the frame. Make sure it is centered between the brake pads or the chainstay and seatstay. Tighten the quick release or axle nuts firmly. Reconnect the brake, then spin the wheel to check that it does not rub.

## Common mistakes

- Pinched tube: a line of two small holes from the lever. Let the air out and reseat the tire more carefully.
- Valve at the wrong angle: the tube will bulge near the valve. Check that the tube sits square.
- Forgetting to tighten the wheel: the wheel can slip or come loose while you ride.

## After you get home

Find the leak with water. Clean and dry the tube. Check the tire carefully for the cause of the puncture.

# Roadside Tube Patch Guide

This guide walks you through fixing a flat inner tube on the road. Allow 20 to 30 minutes the first time.

## What you need

- Tire levers (2 or 3, plastic is fine)
- A patch kit (glue, patches, sandpaper or a scuffer)
- A pump or CO2 inflator
- A spare tube, if you have one (swapping is often faster than patching)
- A small bowl of water or your eyes, to find the hole
- A rag or shirt to wipe the rim and tube

## Step 1: Stop and secure the bike

Flip the bike onto its saddle and handlebars, or lean it against a fence or tree with the wheel free. If the bike has a rear flat, shift into the smallest rear cog to ease removing the wheel.

## Step 2: Remove the wheel

- Rear wheel: open the quick release lever on the axle (or loosen the axle nuts with a wrench). Pull the chain off the rear cog if needed, then lift the wheel out.
- Front wheel: open the quick release or loosen the axle nuts, then lift the wheel out.

Do not squeeze the brake levers while the wheel is out.

## Step 3: Let the air out

Press the valve core on the tube tip with a fingernail, or unscrew the valve cap and press the pin. Squeeze the tire to push out any remaining air.

## Step 4: Remove the tire

1. Push one bead (the tire edge) off the rim on the side opposite the valve. Work it toward the center of the rim with your hands first.
2. Hook a tire lever under the bead and pry it up and over the rim edge.
3. Hook a second lever a few spokes away from the first, and pry the bead over again.
4. Slide the first lever along the rim to lift the whole bead off.
5. Pull the valve out of its hole in the rim, then pull the tube out from under the tire.

Keep the tire on the bike if you can. You only need to free one side to reach the tube.

## Step 5: Find the hole

1. Pump the tube up slightly so it has shape. Listen for a hiss.
2. Run your hand slowly along the tube, feeling for air or bumps.
3. If you still cannot find it, dip sections into water and watch for bubbles.
4. Mark the hole with a pen or a dot of dirt so you can find it again.

Check the inside of the tire for the cause of the flat. Look for glass, thorns, or a sharp stone. Remove anything you find. If you skip this, the new hole will happen again.

## Step 6: Prepare the tube

1. Let the tube deflate fully.
2. Sand a patch sized area around the hole with the sandpaper or scuffer. Roughen it until the surface looks dull and feels slightly fuzzy. Do not sand past the rubber into the fabric.
3. Wipe off the dust with a clean finger or rag. Do not touch the sanded spot again.

## Step 7: Apply the glue

1. Squeeze a thin, even layer of glue over the sanded area. Use just enough to cover the patch footprint.
2. Let the glue get tacky. Most glues take 1 to 3 minutes. It should feel slightly sticky and not wet when you touch the edge with a clean finger.

## Step 8: Apply the patch

1. Peel the foil off the back of the patch. Do not touch the sticky side.
2. Center the patch over the hole.
3. Press firmly from the center outward for 30 to 60 seconds. Use your thumb or the flat of a lever.
4. Leave the foil on top if your kit says to. Some patches have a plastic cover.

Wait the time shown on the kit, usually 2 to 5 minutes, before handling the tube hard.

## Step 9: Check the tube before refitting

1. Lightly pump the tube to see its shape.
2. Check the patch edges. They should lie flat with no lifting.
3. Test the patch with water or by listening for hiss again. If it leaks, you can apply another patch over the first one after cleaning and sanding again.

## Step 10: Refit the tube

1. Pump the tube a little so it holds its round shape. Do not inflate it fully yet.
2. Put the tube inside the tire. Start the valve in the rim hole first, then tuck the rest of the tube in.
3. Make sure the tube is not twisted and sits evenly between the tire beads.
4. Push the tire bead back onto the rim, starting opposite the valve and finishing near the valve.
5. For the last few inches, use your thumbs. Avoid tire levers here, because they can pinch the tube and cause a new flat.
6. Check that the tube is not caught under the bead on either side.

## Step 11: Inflate

1. Push the valve stem up through the rim hole so the tire sits evenly.
2. Inflate in short bursts, checking that the bead stays seated on the rim.
3. Inflate to the pressure marked on the tire sidewall (for example, 80 to 100 psi on a road tire). If you do not have a gauge, squeeze the tire firmly. It should feel hard with little give.
4. If you hear a loud bang or see a bulge, stop and deflate. The tube may be pinched.

## Step 12: Reinstall the wheel

1. Line up the wheel in the dropouts. For a rear wheel, put the chain back on the smallest cog first, then the wheel.
2. Close the quick release or tighten the axle nuts. For a quick release, the lever should leave a firm hand mark on your palm when closed.
3. Spin the wheel and check that it runs straight without rubbing the brake pads or frame.
4. Squeeze the brakes and check that they still stop the wheel.

## Step 13: Ride carefully

# Roadside Tube Patch Guide

This guide walks you through fixing a flat inner tube on the road. Allow 20 to 30 minutes the first time.

## What you need

- Tire levers (2 or 3, plastic is fine)
- A patch kit (glue, patches, sandpaper or a scuffer)
- A pump or CO2 inflator
- A spare tube, if you have one (swapping is often faster than patching)
- A small bowl of water or your eyes, to find the hole
- A rag or shirt to wipe the rim and tube

## Step 1: Stop and secure the bike

Flip the bike onto its saddle and handlebars, or lean it against a fence or tree with the wheel free. If the bike has a rear flat, shift into the smallest rear cog to ease removing the wheel.

## Step 2: Remove the wheel

- Rear wheel: open the quick release lever on the axle (or loosen the axle nuts with a wrench). Pull the chain off the rear cog if needed, then lift the wheel out.
- Front wheel: open the quick release or loosen the axle nuts, then lift the wheel out.

Do not squeeze the brake levers while the wheel is out.

## Step 3: Let the air out

Press the valve core on the tube tip with a fingernail, or unscrew the valve cap and press the pin. Squeeze the tire to push out any remaining air.

## Step 4: Remove the tire

1. Push one bead (the tire edge) off the rim on the side opposite the valve. Work it toward the center of the rim with your hands first.
2. Hook a tire lever under the bead and pry it up and over the rim edge.
3. Hook a second lever a few spokes away from the first, and pry the bead over again.
4. Slide the first lever along the rim to lift the whole bead off.
5. Pull the valve out of its hole in the rim, then pull the tube out from under the tire.

Keep the tire on the bike if you can. You only need to free one side to reach the tube.

## Step 5: Find the hole

1. Pump the tube up slightly so it has shape. Listen for a hiss.
2. Run your hand slowly along the tube, feeling for air or bumps.
3. If you still cannot find it, dip sections into water and watch for bubbles.
4. Mark the hole with a pen or a dot of dirt so you can find it again.

Check the inside of the tire for the cause of the flat. Look for glass, thorns, or a sharp stone. Remove anything you find. If you skip this, the new hole will happen again.

## Step 6: Prepare the tube

1. Let the tube deflate fully.
2. Sand a patch sized area around the hole with the sandpaper or scuffer. Roughen it until the surface looks dull and feels slightly fuzzy. Do not sand past the rubber into the fabric.
3. Wipe off the dust with a clean finger or rag. Do not touch the sanded spot again.

## Step 7: Apply the glue

1. Squeeze a thin, even layer of glue over the sanded area. Use just enough to cover the patch footprint.
2. Let the glue get tacky. Most glues take 1 to 3 minutes. It should feel slightly sticky and not wet when you touch the edge with a clean finger.

## Step 8: Apply the patch

1. Peel the foil off the back of the patch. Do not touch the sticky side.
2. Center the patch over the hole.
3. Press firmly from the center outward for 30 to 60 seconds. Use your thumb or the flat of a lever.
4. Leave the foil on top if your kit says to. Some patches have a plastic cover.

Wait the time shown on the kit, usually 2 to 5 minutes, before handling the tube hard.

## Step 9: Check the tube before refitting

1. Lightly pump the tube to see its shape.
2. Check the patch edges. They should lie flat with no lifting.
3. Test the patch with water or by listening for hiss again. If it leaks, you can apply another patch over the first one after cleaning and sanding again.

## Step 10: Refit the tube

1. Pump the tube a little so it holds its round shape. Do not inflate it fully yet.
2. Put the tube inside the tire. Start the valve in the rim hole first, then tuck the rest of the tube in.
3. Make sure the tube is not twisted and sits evenly between the tire beads.
4. Push the tire bead back onto the rim, starting opposite the valve and finishing near the valve.
5. For the last few inches, use your thumbs. Avoid tire levers here, because they can pinch the tube and cause a new flat.
6. Check that the tube is not caught under the bead on either side.

## Step 11: Inflate

1. Push the valve stem up through the rim hole so the tire sits evenly.
2. Inflate in short bursts, checking that the bead stays seated on the rim.
3. Inflate to the pressure marked on the tire sidewall (for example, 80 to 100 psi on a road tire). If you do not have a gauge, squeeze the tire firmly. It should feel hard with little give.
4. If you hear a loud bang or see a bulge, stop and deflate. The tube may be pinched.

## Step 12: Reinstall the wheel

1. Line up the wheel in the dropouts. For a rear wheel, put the chain back on the smallest cog first, then the wheel.
2. Close the quick release or tighten the axle nuts. For a quick release, the lever should leave a firm hand mark on your palm when closed.
3. Spin the wheel and check that it runs straight without rubbing the brake pads or frame.
4. Squeeze the brakes and check that they still stop the wheel.

## Step 13: Ride carefully

Ride slowly for the first few minutes. Stop and check that the tire is still seated and the pressure has not dropped much. If it went flat again quickly, the patch may have failed or the tube was pinched. Carry a spare tube or a second patch kit.

## Tips

- Always carry a spare tube, a pump or CO2 cartridge, and at least one tire lever.
- Patches are less reliable than new tubes on high-pressure road tires. Use a spare tube when you can, and patch the old one at home.
- Check your tire for embedded glass or thorns before refitting, or the flat will return.

chat: Torque wrenches tighten fasteners to a specific torque, the rotational force measured in newton-metres or foot-pounds. Bolts that are too loose can back out, and bolts that are too tight can stretch or strip threads. Bike work uses them most for stem, handlebar, seatpost, crank, and disc brake bolts, which often have printed torque limits. Click-type and beam-type wrenches are the common styles.

# Week-Long Bike Tour Packing Guide

This guide lists what to pack for a seven-day self-supported bike tour, with the reason for each item. Pack the bike and gear in a way that lets you check the bike as luggage and carry the rest on the plane.

## 1. Travel with the bike

- Bike box or soft bag. Airlines usually charge a fee for bikes, and a box protects the frame and derailleur better than a soft bag. Ask the airline about size and weight limits before you pack.
- Pedals removed, handlebars turned and wrapped, seat post dropped. These steps shrink the bike so it fits in the box and stops parts from snapping during transit.
- Foam pipe insulation over the frame tubes and bubble wrap over the derailleur. Padding stops scratches and cracks.
- Thru axle or wheel spacers and a zip tie to hold the front wheel. Keeps the wheel from moving and damaging the frame.
- Multi tool with the correct hex keys, chain tool, and tire levers in your carry-on. Baggage handling may separate the bike from your tools, and you need them to rebuild the bike at the start.
- Spare tube, patch kit, and a small pump or CO2 inflator in your carry-on. Lithium and CO2 rules vary, so check the airline policy for sealed inflators.
- Printed copy of the bike box dimensions and the airline bike policy.

## 2. Bike spares and tools

- Two spare tubes that fit your wheel size and valve type. Tubes are the most common roadside failure.
- Tire boots or a dollar bill for sidewall cuts.
- Chain quick link matched to your chain speed (for example 11 speed or 12 speed). A broken chain is hard to fix without the right link.
- Brake pads, spare cables, and a derailleur hanger if your bike uses one. Hangers bend in crashes and stop shifting.
- Lube for the chain and a rag. A dry chain wears fast and makes noise.
- Full-size floor pump for the hotel or cooperative bike shop stops.
- Spoke wrench. A loose spoke can ruin a wheel on long rides.

## 3. Clothing for riding

- Three to four cycling jerseys. Wool or synthetic fabrics dry faster than cotton and handle sweat well.
- Three pairs of padded cycling shorts. Rotate them to let each pair dry and air out between rides. Padding reduces saddle soreness over many hours.
- Two to three pairs of cycling socks. Wool socks prevent blisters and handle wet conditions.
- Arm warmers and leg warmers. They add warmth in cool mornings and come off as the day warms up.
- Lightweight rain jacket and rain pants or shell. Rain happens on tours even in dry seasons.
- Warm layer such as a thin fleece or down vest. Descents and early mornings get cold, and wind chill adds to the drop.
- Gloves, one pair of full finger and one pair of fingerless. Protects hands in a crash and from wind chill.
- Cap or buff for sun and cold.
- Sunglasses with clear or yellow lenses for dusk and rain.

## 4. Off-bike clothing

- Two or three casual outfits. Off-bike clothes give your cycling kit a rest and suit restaurants and shops.
- Comfortable shoes or sandals for walking and for days when cleats hurt.
- Sleepwear and one set of underwear per day. Underwear and socks are light, quick to wash, and dry overnight.
- Swimwear if you expect to use hotel pools or rivers.

## 5. Shoes and footwear

- Cycling shoes and spare cleat bolts. Cleats wear and bolts can loosen.
- Lightweight camp shoes or sandals. These are useful for showers and hostels.

## 6. Sleep and shelter (if camping or hostelling)

- Tent or hostel sleep sheet. Confirm what each night will require before you leave.
- Sleeping bag rated for the lowest expected temperature, plus a sleeping pad. A pad insulates you from cold ground and protects you from roots and stones.
- Pillow or inflatable pillow for sleep quality.
- Headlamp with spare batteries. Good for camp chores and for riding in the dark.

## 7. Bags and packing

- Saddle bag or seat pack for tools and a spare tube.
- Handlebar bag for snacks, phone, and wallet.
- Frame bag if your bike has the mounts. Holds heavy items low for stability.
- Panniers or a rear rack bag if you carry gear on the bike. Balance weight evenly between left and right.
- Dry bags or packing cubes. Protect clothing and electronics from rain and spills.
- Compression sacks for sleeping bag and extra layers.

## 8. Electronics

- Phone with a mount and a USB cable. Navigation, camera, and emergency calls depend on it.
- Power bank with at least 10000 mAh. One full charge may not last a long day with navigation running.
- Wall charger and a short extension cord or multi-port charger. Hotels have few outlets.
- Adapter for the destination country.
- Bike computer or GPS unit with a charger, if you use one.
- Waterproof phone pouch.

## 9. Navigation and documents

- Offline maps saved on the phone, plus a paper route sheet or cue sheet. Signal drops in rural areas.
- Passport, ID, travel insurance card, and emergency contacts on paper. Documents may need to be shown at borders and hospitals.
- Credit card and some cash in local currency. Some small towns take only cash.
- Printed hotel and campsite reservations for each night.
- Map case or waterproof map holder.

## 10. Health and first aid

- Personal medications in original packaging, with a copy of the prescription.
- First aid kit with bandages, antiseptic wipes, blister plasters, and pain relief. Blisters and road rash are the most common tour injuries.
- Sunscreen, lip balm with SPF, and insect repellent.
- Anti-diarrheal and rehydration salts. Stomach upsets are common when eating in new places.
- Chamois cream. Reduces chafing on long days in the saddle.
- Personal hygiene items in small containers.

## 11. Food and hydration

- Two water bottles plus a bottle cage for each. Water needs on hot days can exceed two liters per hour.
- Water filter or purification tablets if you expect to refill from streams or taps you do not trust.
- Electrolyte tablets or powder. Sweat loss depletes sodium and potassium.
- Energy bars, gels, or chews for the ride. Bonking happens fast when calories run out.
- Light snacks for camp or rest stops.

## 12. Repair and emergency

- Reflective gear and lights, front and rear. Visibility keeps you safe on roads, in traffic, and at dusk.
- Whistle and small emergency blanket. Useful if you break down or get stranded.
- Small notebook and pen for route notes and contacts.
- Duct tape wrapped around a pencil or stored on the frame. Works as a quick patch for many problems.
- Zip ties and a few spare bolts of common sizes.

## 13. Toiletries and miscellaneous

- Microfiber towel. Dries fast and packs small.
- Toothbrush, toothpaste, and soap in small bottles or bars.
- Sunglasses case or hard case for protection.
- Earplugs and eye mask for sleep in noisy hostels.
- Laundry detergent sheets for washing kit each evening.
- Plastic bags for wet or dirty clothes.

## 14. Before you leave

- Fit check: ride your bike fully loaded for at least one short trip. Adjust for balance and comfort before the tour.
- Test the bike box: confirm it closes and the bike stays secure inside.
- Weigh your bags at home to confirm the airline weight limit.
- Save a digital copy of this list and your bookings to the phone while you still have internet access.
- Share your route and expected arrival times with someone at home.

## Packing order for the day before the flight

1. Assemble the bike box and place the bike inside with spacers and padding.
2. Pack the tools, spares, and first aid kit in carry-on.
3. Fill the bike box with the bags that go on the bike, but keep fragile items in carry-on.
4. Check total weight and confirm documents are in your carry-on.

# Week Long Bike Tour Packing Guide

This guide assumes a self supported tour with panniers, camping or hostel stays, and daily riding of 50 to 90 km. Adjust quantities if you have a support vehicle or stay in hotels every night.

## 1. Bike and safety kit

These items keep you riding. Missing one can end the trip.

- Helmet. Required on most routes and the main protection in a crash.
- Front and rear lights, charged, plus spare batteries. Riding at dusk or in tunnels is common on tours.
- Two spare inner tubes, matching your wheel size, plus a spare tire if your tires are worn. Punctures are the most common roadside failure.
- Tire levers (2 or 3) and a patch kit. Levers and patches fix a flat when the tube is damaged beyond a quick swap.
- Hand pump or compact pump, tested before departure. A CO2 inflator is quick but gives only one fill per cartridge.
- Multitool with hex keys, a chain breaker, and a spoke wrench. Covers most adjustments and a broken chain link.
- Quick link for your chain model. A broken chain without a quick link means a long walk.
- Spare brake pads for your brake type. Worn pads on a long descent are a safety risk.
- Spare derailleur hanger if your frame uses a replaceable one. A bent hanger can lock the drivetrain.
- Cable ties and a few zip ties. They fix a loose rack, a bent fender, or a snapped cable.
- Spare brake and shift cable, if you know how to fit it. Cables stretch and fray over a week of use.
- Chain lube for the conditions you expect, plus a rag. A dry chain wears fast and shifts poorly.
- Bike lock. Use it at every stop, even in small towns.
- Water bottles or a hydration bladder, two minimum. Carrying 1 to 1.5 liters per riding hour in hot weather prevents heat illness.
- Bike computer or phone mount, with a charged power bank for it.

## 2. Clothing for riding

- Two cycling kits (bib shorts and jersey). Rotate them so one dries while you wear the other. Chamois padding needs a clean kit to avoid saddle sores.
- One long sleeve base layer for cold mornings and descents.
- Lightweight rain jacket, packable. It blocks wind and rain and weighs little.
- Arm warmers or a light wind vest. Easy to remove as the day warms up.
- Cycling socks, three pairs. Synthetic or wool dries fast and avoids blisters.
- Cycling gloves. They protect your palms in a fall and cut vibration on rough roads.
- Sunglasses with a spare lens or a clear lens for overcast or dusk riding. Eye protection stops grit and bugs.
- Cycling cap or buff for sun and sweat.
- Shoes with a good sole for walking off the bike. Clip in shoes are hard to walk in, so some riders bring flat shoes too.

## 3. Clothing off the bike

- Two light shirts and one warm layer for evenings. Evenings in mountains or coastal areas can drop 10 degrees or more.
- One pair of shorts or light pants for town and rest days.
- Underwear and socks, one set per day plus one spare.
- Sleep clothes that you do not ride in.
- Sandals or camp shoes for showers and rest stops.
- Sun hat for the afternoon heat.

## 4. Camping or lodging gear

Skip this section if you book hotels or guesthouses for every night.

- Tent with footprint, or a bivy and tarp. Check the tent fits in a pannier or on the rack.
- Sleeping bag rated 5 degrees C below the coldest expected night. Cold nights are more dangerous than warm ones because they cause poor sleep and fatigue.
- Sleeping pad. It insulates you from the ground and cushions your back.
- Small pillow or stuff sack filled with clothes.
- Headlamp with spare batteries. Hands free light for camp chores.
- Small stove, fuel, and a pot. Check local rules on fuel carriage before you fly.
- Lighter or matches, in a waterproof case.
- Water filter or purification tablets. Confirm the water source is safe for each stop.
- Reusable bowl, spork, and a small cup.
- Dry bag or waterproof stuff sacks for the sleeping bag and clothes. Rain soaks a bag quickly and wet gear is heavy and cold.

## 5. Health and hygiene

- Sunscreen SPF 30 or higher, and lip balm with SPF. Sun exposure on a bike lasts for hours.
- Chamois cream. It reduces friction and chafing on long days.
- Anti chafe balm for thighs and underarms.
- Blister kit: moleskin, tape, and a small needle. Blisters on day two can ruin the rest of the week.
- Ibuprofen or acetaminophen. Use with care, and avoid taking it before hard efforts if you have kidney concerns.
- Antihistamine and any prescription medicine, in the original containers with a copy of the prescription.
- Electrolyte tablets or powder. Sweat loss in heat can cause cramps and headaches.
- Basic first aid kit with bandages, antiseptic wipes, gauze, and tweezers.
- Toiletries: toothbrush, toothpaste, deodorant, small soap, and a quick dry towel.
- Hand sanitizer and tissues.
- Insect repellent. Mosquitoes and ticks are common on many routes.
- Personal medical notes: allergies, blood type, and an emergency contact on a card or your phone.

## 6. Electronics and documents

- Phone, with a mount and a case that protects it in a fall.
- Charger, cable, and a power bank of at least 10000 mAh. Carry the power bank in hand luggage, because airlines restrict lithium batteries in checked bags.
- Plug adapter for your destination.
- Headphones or earbuds. Use only one ear while riding so you hear traffic.
- Passport, ID, travel insurance card, and any visas. Keep copies in a separate place.
- Printed or offline map and route notes. Phones lose signal in rural areas, and battery drain is faster in cold weather.
- Cash in local currency, plus one card. Some rural shops take cash only.
- Emergency contact list on paper.

## 7. Packing and organization

- Use two or three panniers at most, with a waterproof liner in each. Balance weight: heavier items low and central, lighter items high or at the back.
- Keep a small top bag or handlebar bag for things you need during the day: snacks, sunscreen, phone, wallet, and rain jacket.
- Pack daily clothes in separate dry bags so each day is easy to find.
- Keep all tools in one kit bag within reach.
- Weigh the loaded bike once before the trip. Aim for a total that your rack and frame rating allow.
- Carry a small bag of snacks: nuts, bars, and dried fruit. Eat every 45 to 60 minutes while riding to avoid bonking.

## 8. Flight and transport

- Remove pedals, turn the handlebars parallel to the frame, lower the saddle, and deflate tires a little. These steps protect the bike and fit it into a bike box or bag.
- Use a padded bike bag or hard case. Wrap the derailleur and disc rotors.
- Check your airline's rules on bike fees, size limits, and whether the bike must be boxed.
- Keep tools and spare parts in your hand luggage if the airline permits them. Airlines usually ban some tools in carry on bags, so confirm before packing.
- Keep a list of tour contacts and a backup plan if the bike arrives damaged.

## 9. Before you leave

- Test ride the loaded bike for at least 30 minutes.
- Check brakes, shifting, tire pressure, and bolt torque.
- Pack your spare tube and tools in the bag you will use on day one, so you can reach them without unpacking.
- Make a one page daily plan with distances, water stops, and emergency numbers.

# Week Long Bike Tour Packing Guide

This guide assumes a self supported tour with panniers, camping or hostel stays, and daily riding of 50 to 90 km. Adjust quantities if you have a support vehicle or stay in hotels every night.

## 1. Bike and safety kit

These items keep you riding. Missing one can end the trip.

- Helmet. Required on most routes and the main protection in a crash.
- Front and rear lights, charged, plus spare batteries. Riding at dusk or in tunnels is common on tours.
- Two spare inner tubes, matching your wheel size, plus a spare tire if your tires are worn. Punctures are the most common roadside failure.
- Tire levers (2 or 3) and a patch kit. Levers and patches fix a flat when the tube is damaged beyond a quick swap.
- Hand pump or compact pump, tested before departure. A CO2 inflator is quick but gives only one fill per cartridge.
- Multitool with hex keys, a chain breaker, and a spoke wrench. Covers most adjustments and a broken chain link.
- Quick link for your chain model. A broken chain without a quick link means a long walk.
- Spare brake pads for your brake type. Worn pads on a long descent are a safety risk.
- Spare derailleur hanger if your frame uses a replaceable one. A bent hanger can lock the drivetrain.
- Cable ties and a few zip ties. They fix a loose rack, a bent fender, or a snapped cable.
- Spare brake and shift cable, if you know how to fit it. Cables stretch and fray over a week of use.
- Chain lube for the conditions you expect, plus a rag. A dry chain wears fast and shifts poorly.
- Bike lock. Use it at every stop, even in small towns.
- Water bottles or a hydration bladder, two minimum. Carrying 1 to 1.5 liters per riding hour in hot weather prevents heat illness.
- Bike computer or phone mount, with a charged power bank for it.

## 2. Clothing for riding

- Two cycling kits (bib shorts and jersey). Rotate them so one dries while you wear the other. Chamois padding needs a clean kit to avoid saddle sores.
- One long sleeve base layer for cold mornings and descents.
- Lightweight rain jacket, packable. It blocks wind and rain and weighs little.
- Arm warmers or a light wind vest. Easy to remove as the day warms up.
- Cycling socks, three pairs. Synthetic or wool dries fast and avoids blisters.
- Cycling gloves. They protect your palms in a fall and cut vibration on rough roads.
- Sunglasses with a spare lens or a clear lens for overcast or dusk riding. Eye protection stops grit and bugs.
- Cycling cap or buff for sun and sweat.
- Shoes with a good sole for walking off the bike. Clip in shoes are hard to walk in, so some riders bring flat shoes too.

## 3. Clothing off the bike

- Two light shirts and one warm layer for evenings. Evenings in mountains or coastal areas can drop 10 degrees or more.
- One pair of shorts or light pants for town and rest days.
- Underwear and socks, one set per day plus one spare.
- Sleep clothes that you do not ride in.
- Sandals or camp shoes for showers and rest stops.
- Sun hat for the afternoon heat.

## 4. Camping or lodging gear

Skip this section if you book hotels or guesthouses for every night.

- Tent with footprint, or a bivy and tarp. Check the tent fits in a pannier or on the rack.
- Sleeping bag rated 5 degrees C below the coldest expected night. Cold nights are more dangerous than warm ones because they cause poor sleep and fatigue.
- Sleeping pad. It insulates you from the ground and cushions your back.
- Small pillow or stuff sack filled with clothes.
- Headlamp with spare batteries. Hands free light for camp chores.
- Small stove, fuel, and a pot. Check local rules on fuel carriage before you fly.
- Lighter or matches, in a waterproof case.
- Water filter or purification tablets. Confirm the water source is safe for each stop.
- Reusable bowl, spork, and a small cup.
- Dry bag or waterproof stuff sacks for the sleeping bag and clothes. Rain soaks a bag quickly and wet gear is heavy and cold.

## 5. Health and hygiene

- Sunscreen SPF 30 or higher, and lip balm with SPF. Sun exposure on a bike lasts for hours.
- Chamois cream. It reduces friction and chafing on long days.
- Anti chafe balm for thighs and underarms.
- Blister kit: moleskin, tape, and a small needle. Blisters on day two can ruin the rest of the week.
- Ibuprofen or acetaminophen. Use with care, and avoid taking it before hard efforts if you have kidney concerns.
- Antihistamine and any prescription medicine, in the original containers with a copy of the prescription.
- Electrolyte tablets or powder. Sweat loss in heat can cause cramps and headaches.
- Basic first aid kit with bandages, antiseptic wipes, gauze, and tweezers.
- Toiletries: toothbrush, toothpaste, deodorant, small soap, and a quick dry towel.
- Hand sanitizer and tissues.
- Insect repellent. Mosquitoes and ticks are common on many routes.
- Personal medical notes: allergies, blood type, and an emergency contact on a card or your phone.

## 6. Electronics and documents

- Phone, with a mount and a case that protects it in a fall.
- Charger, cable, and a power bank of at least 10000 mAh. Carry the power bank in hand luggage, because airlines restrict lithium batteries in checked bags.
- Plug adapter for your destination.
- Headphones or earbuds. Use only one ear while riding so you hear traffic.
- Passport, ID, travel insurance card, and any visas. Keep copies in a separate place.
- Printed or offline map and route notes. Phones lose signal in rural areas, and battery drain is faster in cold weather.
- Cash in local currency, plus one card. Some rural shops take cash only.
- Emergency contact list on paper.

## 7. Packing and organization

- Use two or three panniers at most, with a waterproof liner in each. Balance weight: heavier items low and central, lighter items high or at the back.
- Keep a small top bag or handlebar bag for things you need during the day: snacks, sunscreen, phone, wallet, and rain jacket.
- Pack daily clothes in separate dry bags so each day is easy to find.
- Keep all tools in one kit bag within reach.
- Weigh the loaded bike once before the trip. Aim for a total that your rack and frame rating allow.
- Carry a small bag of snacks: nuts, bars, and dried fruit. Eat every 45 to 60 minutes while riding to avoid bonking.

## 8. Flight and transport

- Remove pedals, turn the handlebars parallel to the frame, lower the saddle, and deflate tires a little. These steps protect the bike and fit it into a bike box or bag.
- Use a padded bike bag or hard case. Wrap the derailleur and disc rotors.
- Check your airline's rules on bike fees, size limits, and whether the bike must be boxed.
- Keep tools and spare parts in your hand luggage if the airline permits them. Airlines usually ban some tools in carry on bags, so confirm before packing.
- Keep a list of tour contacts and a backup plan if the bike arrives damaged.

## 9. Before you leave

- Test ride the loaded bike for at least 30 minutes.
- Check brakes, shifting, tire pressure, and bolt torque.
- Pack your spare tube and tools in the bag you will use on day one, so you can reach them without unpacking.
- Make a one page daily plan with distances, water stops, and emergency numbers.

Full written guide saved at workbench/roadside-tube-patch-guide.md. Short version:

1. Shift to the smallest cog, open the brake quick release, and remove the wheel.
2. Let out the air. Lever the tire bead off the rim, starting by the valve.
3. Pull out the valve, then the tube.
4. Add a little air and find the hole by listening or by watching bubbles in water. Mark it.
5. Feel inside the tire for the cause and remove it.
6. Rough the area around the hole with sandpaper.
7. Spread a thin layer of glue, wait until it is tacky, then press the patch on and hold 30 seconds.
8. Tuck the tube back in, starting with the valve, and seat the bead with your thumbs.
9. Inflate to the sidewall pressure, then refit the wheel and check the brakes.

# Roadside Tube Patch Guide

This guide walks through patching a bike inner tube at the roadside. Read each step before you do it.

## What you need

- Tire levers (two or three, plastic is best)
- A patch kit: rubber cement, sandpaper or a scuffer, and patches
- A pump, or a CO2 cartridge with inflator
- A marker or chalk
- A small bowl of water, or a helper who can listen for air leaks

## Step 1: Stop and get the wheel off

1. Move the bike off the road and stand it up or lay it on its non-drive side.
2. Shift the rear wheel onto the smallest cog if the flat is on the back wheel. This lowers tension on the chain.
3. If the bike has rim brakes, open the brake quick release lever on the caliper. Then the tire clears the brake pads.
4. Open the quick release skewer or undo the axle nuts. Pull the wheel out of the frame. Keep the chain away from the wheel as you lift it.

## Step 2: Let the air out and release the tire bead

1. Unscrew the valve cap. Press the valve pin briefly to release any air still inside.
2. Press the tire bead (the edge of the tire that sits on the rim) into the center channel of the rim on the side opposite the valve. This gives you slack.
3. Push one tire lever under the bead next to the valve. Hook the lever over a spoke so it stays in place.
4. Push a second lever under the bead about 10 cm away. Hook it on a spoke too.
5. Work around the rim with the levers. Only lift the bead out of the rim with one lever at a time, using short moves. Do not pry hard, because you can pinch and cut the tube.

## Step 3: Remove the tube

1. Unscrew the valve nut from the rim hole, then push the valve stem back through the hole.
2. Pull the tube out of the tire, starting at the valve.
3. Keep the tire on the rim if you can. You can check the inside of the tire later.

## Step 4: Find the hole

1. Put a little air in the tube until it holds a shape. Do not inflate it fully.
2. Listen for a hiss. Run your fingers slowly along the tube. Or hold the tube in a bowl of water and watch for bubbles.
3. Mark the hole with your marker or chalk. Mark a circle around it so you can find it again.
4. Let the air out.

## Step 5: Check for the cause

1. Look inside the tire, using your fingers gently around the inside. Feel for a thorn, glass, or wire.
2. Remove anything you find. If you leave it in, the new patch will fail.
3. Check the rim. A spoke end or a rim edge with no rim tape can pierce the tube. Smooth it with a file or cover it with rim tape if you have some.

## Step 6: Roughen the area around the hole

1. Use the sandpaper or scuffer from the kit. Rub a patch-sized area around the hole, about 2 cm past it on each side.
2. The surface should look dull and rough. Brush off the dust. Do not touch the roughened spot with your fingers, because oil stops the glue from bonding.

## Step 7: Apply glue and patch

1. Squeeze a thin layer of rubber cement onto the roughened area. Spread it a little larger than the patch. Use a thin coat, not a thick blob.
2. Wait until the glue is tacky. It should feel sticky but not wet on your fingertip. This usually takes 1 to 2 minutes. Follow the time on the kit.
3. Peel the foil backing off the patch. Do not touch the sticky side.
4. Place the patch centered over the hole. Press it down firmly from the center outward to push out air bubbles.
5. Hold the patch down for about 30 seconds.

## Step 8: Put the tube back in the tire

1. Put a small amount of air in the tube so it takes shape. This makes it easier to fit.
2. Check the tire inside. Make sure nothing sharp is left in it.
3. Push the valve stem into the rim hole first. Then tuck the tube into the tire all the way around. Keep it inside the tire, with no folds pinched between the tire and rim.
4. Starting at the valve, push the tire bead back onto the rim by hand. Work toward the opposite side. Use your thumbs, not levers, for the last section. Levers can pinch the tube.
5. Check that the tire sits evenly on both sides of the rim. No tube should show along the edge.

## Step 9: Inflate and check

1. Screw the valve nut back on the stem, snug it up, and put the valve cap on.
2. Inflate slowly. Watch the tire bead to make sure it sits evenly. Stop if one side bulges.
3. Inflate to the pressure printed on the tire sidewall. Do not exceed the maximum.
4. Spin the wheel and listen. Look for rubbing or a wobble.

## Step 10: Put the wheel back on

1. Line up the wheel in the frame with the axle fully seated in the dropouts.
2. Tighten the quick release or axle nuts firmly.
3. Close the brake quick release and check that the pads sit evenly on the rim.
4. Spin the wheel. Check that it runs true and does not rub the brakes or frame.
5. Check that the chain sits on the right gear, and shift through a few gears.

## If the patch does not hold

- If you hear hissing or the tire goes soft again, the patch may have leaked. Repeat Steps 4 to 7 with a fresh patch.
- If you do not have a patch kit or the patch fails, use a spare tube if you carry one. Patch the old tube later at home.
- If you have no spare tube and no patch, a folded bank note or a dry leaf placed inside the tire over the cut can protect the tube enough to ride home slowly. Check the tire often and keep the pressure low.

## Safety

- Do not ride on a patch that bulges or looks loose.
- Do not inflate past the maximum pressure on the sidewall.
- If the tire has a large cut or the bead is damaged, replace the tire before riding far.

# Patching a Bike Tube at the Roadside

This guide takes about 30 to 45 minutes the first time. Read all steps before you start.

## What you need

1. Tire levers (two or three plastic levers are best)
2. A patch kit: patches, rubber cement, and a small sandpaper or rasp
3. A pump, or a CO2 cartridge with inflator
4. A marker or pen
5. A dollar bill or a folded wrapper, only as an emergency tire boot

## Step 1: Get the wheel off

1. Shift the chain onto the smallest rear cog. This loosens the chain so the wheel comes out easily.
2. If the brake is a caliper brake with a quick release lever, open the lever. Rim brakes also often have a release tab on the arm.
3. Open the quick release on the wheel, or loosen the axle nuts with a wrench.
4. Lift the wheel out. For a rear wheel, lift the chain off the cog while you pull the wheel back.

## Step 2: Let the air out

1. Find the valve. A thin skinny valve with a small top nut is a Presta valve. A fatter valve with a spring is a Schrader valve.
2. Presta: unscrew the top nut, then press the pin in the tip briefly to release air.
3. Schrader: press the pin in the center with a fingernail or the tip of a key.
4. Squeeze the tire until it is soft all the way around.

## Step 3: Remove one side of the tire

1. Push the bead, which is the stiff edge of the tire, toward the center of the rim along the spot opposite the valve.
2. Slide the flat tip of a lever under the bead. Hook the lever onto a spoke so it stays put.
3. Insert a second lever a hand width away, under the bead, and pry it up. Hook it to a spoke too.
4. Run the first lever around the rim one spoke at a time to free the bead.
5. Pull the bead off the rim on one side.

## Step 4: Remove the tube

1. Pull the valve out of the rim hole first.
2. Pull the rest of the tube out from under the tire.
3. Keep the tire on the rim if you can. You can leave the second bead on the rim.

## Step 5: Find the hole

1. Add a little air to the tube, just enough to round it out.
2. Run your hand slowly along the tube and listen for hissing. You can also feel for air on your cheek.
3. If you still cannot find it, dip a section into water and watch for bubbles.
4. Mark the hole with a pen or a dot of marker.
5. Let all the air out again before patching.

## Step 6: Check the tire for the cause

1. Run your fingers slowly along the inside of the tire. Feel for glass, thorns, or wire.
2. Remove anything you find. Pull it out in the same direction it went in.
3. If the tire has a cut, put a dollar bill or folded wrapper between the tube and the cut. This stops the tube from poking through.

## Step 7: Prepare the patch area

1. Roughen the area around the hole, about the size of a coin or larger, with sandpaper or the rasp. Scratch the surface until it looks dull.
2. Brush off the dust. Do not touch the roughened spot with your fingers.

## Step 8: Glue the patch

1. Open the rubber cement. Spread a thin, even layer over the roughened area. Do not use too much.
2. Wait until the glue is tacky. This means it feels sticky, not wet. This usually takes 1 to 3 minutes. Follow the label on your kit.
3. Peel the backing off the patch. Do not touch the sticky side.
4. Place the patch over the hole, centered.
5. Press firmly with your thumb for at least 30 seconds. Push from the center to the edges to remove air pockets.
6. Wait a few minutes for the glue to set before the next step.

## Step 9: Put the tube back in the tire

1. Add a small amount of air to the tube so it keeps its shape.
2. Start with the valve. Push the tube in the rim hole so the valve stands straight out.
3. Push the tube into the tire, working around. Keep it from twisting.
4. Make sure no part of the tube sticks out from under the tire edge.

## Step 10: Seat the tire

1. Push the tire bead back onto the rim with your hands. Start at the point opposite the valve and work toward it.
2. Use the levers only for the last section if needed. Be careful not to pinch the tube under the lever. A pinched tube will flat again right away.
3. Check that the tire sits evenly on both sides, with no bulge.

## Step 11: Inflate

1. Check the sidewall of the tire for the recommended pressure, printed as PSI or bar.
2. Inflate slowly to a firm feel. Stop at or below that pressure. Do not exceed the printed maximum.
3. Spin the wheel and watch the tire for a wobble. A wobble can mean the bead is not seated.

## Step 12: Reinstall the wheel

1. Put the wheel back in the frame, with the axle fully in the dropouts.
2. Tighten the quick release or the axle nuts firmly.
3. Lift the chain onto the cog if you took it off. Check the wheel spins freely and the brake pads sit on the rim.
4. Close the brake caliper or reset the brake release.

## After the repair

1. Ride gently for a few minutes and check the tire is still firm.
2. Carry a spare tube or this patch kit for the rest of your ride.
3. A patch is a temporary fix. Replace the tube or have the tire checked at the shop when you can.
