# Torque Wrenches and Bike Torque Values

## What a torque wrench does

A torque wrench lets you tighten a bolt to a set force, measured in newton metres (Nm) in most bike work. Hand tightening guesses the force. Guessing too little lets parts loosen while riding. Guessing too much can crush carbon fibre, strip threads, stretch bolts, or bend parts out of shape.

Two types are common in a shop:

- Click type: a spring-loaded mechanism clicks when the set value is reached. It is simple and accurate for most jobs.
- Beam type: a pointer moves along a scale. It is cheap and reliable, but you must read the scale at eye level.

A torque wrench measures only the force you apply. Its accuracy depends on calibration, so check it on a regular schedule.

Torque limits matter most for three reasons:

1. Clamp force holds parts in place. A stem, seatpost, or handlebar that is too loose can slip under load.
2. Thread damage and stretch. Over-tightened bolts strip threads or stretch, which weakens them.
3. Carbon fibre. Carbon parts can crack or crush when clamped too hard. Carbon parts often list a lower maximum than metal parts.

Always check the markings on the part first. Manufacturer values override these general ranges.

## Common torque values across a whole bike

These are typical ranges for common components. Confirm against the marking on the part or the manufacturer manual before you tighten.

### Cockpit

| Part | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Stem faceplate bolts | 4 to 6 Nm | Clamps the handlebar. Too loose lets the bar rotate. Too tight can crack carbon steerers or stems. |
| Stem steerer expander bolt | 4 to 6 Nm, or per stem | Locks the stem to the fork steerer. Often set with the top cap preload procedure. |
| Handlebar clamp bolts | 4 to 5 Nm, carbon bars 5 to 6 Nm | Holds the bar in the stem. Carbon bars need an even, moderate clamp. |
| Brake lever clamp bolt | 4 to 5 Nm | Stops the lever rotating on the bar. |
| Shifter clamp bolt | 2 to 4 Nm | Holds the shifter. Too tight can damage the bar or shifter body. |
| Cable pinch bolts | 4 to 5 Nm | Holds brake and shift cables. Over-tightening can crush the cable. |

### Seat and frame

| Part | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Seatpost clamp bolt | 5 to 6 Nm, carbon posts per marking | Holds the post at height. Loose posts slip. Carbon posts can crush. |
| Saddle rail clamp | 4 to 6 Nm | Holds the saddle to the post. Loose rails let the saddle twist. |
| Water bottle cage bolts | 4 to 5 Nm, often lower on carbon frames | Holds the cage. Over-tightening can crack carbon bosses. |
| Rack or fender mounts | 4 to 5 Nm | Holds accessories. Too tight can strip threads on alloy frames. |

### Brakes

| Part | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Post mount caliper bolts | 6 to 8 Nm | Holds the caliper to the frame. Loose calipers shift and rub. |
| IS (flat mount) caliper bolts | 8 to 10 Nm | Same job, larger mount. |
| Six-bolt rotor bolts | 2 to 4 Nm | Holds the rotor to the hub. Use a star pattern. |
| Centre lock rotor lockring | 40 Nm | Holds the rotor on the hub splines. |

### Drivetrain

| Part | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Crank bolt (Hollowtech, Octalink, or similar) | 35 to 50 Nm | Holds the crank on the spindle. Loose cranks damage the spindle and the crank. |
| Bottom bracket, threaded | 35 to 50 Nm | Holds the cups in the frame. Check the frame thread type. |
| Pedals | 30 to 35 Nm | Holds the pedal in the crank. Left pedal has a reverse thread. Grease the threads. |
| Chainring bolts | 8 to 12 Nm | Holds rings to the crank arms. Tighten in a star pattern. |
| Cassette lockring | 30 to 50 Nm | Holds the cassette on the freehub. Loose cassettes spin and damage the freehub. |
| Derailleur hanger bolt | 5 to 8 Nm | Holds the derailleur to the frame. Loose hangers shift the gears badly. |
| Derailleur cable bolt | 4 to 5 Nm | Holds the cable at the derailleur. |

### Wheels

| Part | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Thru axle, front or rear | 10 to 15 Nm | Holds the wheel in the fork or frame. Under-tightening lets the wheel shift. |
| Quick release skewer | No torque value. Close firmly by hand, with lever resistance matched to the skewer. | Clamp force comes from the lever, not a bolt. |

## Tips for working safely

- Set the wrench to the lower end of the range first, then increase if needed.
- Tighten bolts in a star or cross pattern where several bolts clamp one part.
- Clean and grease threads only when the manufacturer calls for it. Grease changes the torque reading, so manufacturers often list a separate value for greased threads.
- Do not use a torque wrench to loosen bolts. Impact or sudden force can damage the wrench.
- Replace carbon parts that show cracks, crush marks, or clamp damage.

## Source note

These ranges reflect common published values from major component makers and general shop practice. They are not exact for every product. Check the part marking and the manufacturer manual for each job.

# Torque Wrench Guide for Bicycles

## What a torque wrench is for

A torque wrench measures how hard you tighten a fastener. Most bike bolts are small, and the right tightness is a narrow window. Too loose, and parts move, rattle, or come off. Too tight, and threads strip, aluminum or carbon parts crack or crush, and bolts stretch and lose clamping force.

Bike parts list their torque in newton metres (Nm). Many also show a torque value stamped on the part. Always follow the marking or the manufacturer's manual when it differs from this guide.

Two useful habits:

- Set the wrench to the target value, then tighten in a smooth pull until it clicks or the dial reaches the number. Do not overshoot and back off.
- Use a clean, dry thread unless the manufacturer calls for grease or carbon assembly paste. Lubricant changes the torque a bolt reaches, so a dry torque value applied to a greased bolt can over-tighten it.

Carbon parts need extra care. Carbon does not yield gently like aluminum. Overtightening can crack the part without warning, so use the lower end of the range and check the carbon manufacturer's limit.

## Common torque values across a bike

These are typical values for many road, gravel, and mountain bikes. Treat them as a starting point and confirm against the part.

### Cockpit (handlebars and controls)

| Fastener | Typical torque | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Stem steerer clamp bolts | 5 to 6 Nm | Clamps the stem to the steerer. Too loose lets the bars rotate. Too tight can crush a carbon steerer. |
| Stem faceplate bolts | 4 to 5 Nm | Clamps the handlebar in the stem. Overtightening can crack carbon bars. |
| Handlebar to stem clamp | 5 to 6 Nm | Holds bars straight and secure. Carbon bars often max out at 5 Nm. |
| Brake lever clamp | 4 to 6 Nm | Keeps the lever from slipping on the bar. |
| Shifter or bar-end clamp | 2 to 5 Nm | Keeps shifters aligned. Light torque avoids crushing the bar. |
| Headset top cap or preload bolt | Snug, not a fixed value, usually 2 Nm or less on the cap | Sets bearing preload. Overtightening stresses the bearings and steerer. |

### Seat and seatpost

| Fastener | Typical torque | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Seatpost clamp bolt | 5 to 6 Nm | Holds the post at height. Carbon posts need the lower end. |
| Saddle rail clamp (to post) | 5 to 6 Nm | Holds the saddle angle and position. |

### Brakes

| Fastener | Typical torque | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Rim brake caliper mount | 6 to 8 Nm | Keeps the caliper centered and pad alignment stable. |
| Disc brake caliper mount (flat mount) | 6 to 8 Nm | Holds the caliper square to the rotor. |
| Disc brake caliper mount (IS or post mount) | 8 to 10 Nm | Carries braking load. Check the frame or fork spec. |
| Disc rotor bolts (six-bolt) | 2 to 4 Nm | Attaches the rotor to the hub. Too tight can warp the rotor. |
| Disc rotor center lock ring | About 40 Nm | Locks the rotor to the hub. Shimano lists 40 Nm. Check the hub spec. |

### Wheels

| Fastener | Typical torque | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Thru axle (front) | 8 to 15 Nm | Clamps the wheel in the fork. Under-torque lets the wheel move under braking. |
| Thru axle (rear) | 12 to 15 Nm | Clamps the wheel in the frame. Check the frame spec, since values vary. |
| Quick release | Set by lever feel, not torque | Cam pressure, not torque, holds the wheel. Adjust the cam so the lever closes with firm resistance. |

### Drivetrain

| Fastener | Typical torque | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Crank arm bolt (square taper or Hollowtech) | 35 to 50 Nm | Holds the crank to the spindle. Loose cranks wear the taper and can detach. |
| Hollowtech pinch bolt | About 12 Nm | Clamps the crank arm to the spindle interface. Follow the crank spec. |
| Chainring bolts | 8 to 12 Nm | Holds chainrings to the crank. Uneven torque can cause ring wobble. |
| Cassette lockring | 30 to 50 Nm | Holds the cassette on the freehub. Loose lockrings cause shifting problems and damage. |
| Bottom bracket (threaded) | 35 to 50 Nm | Holds the cups in the shell. Check the cup type. |
| Front derailleur clamp | 5 to 6 Nm | Holds the derailleur on the seat tube. Overtightening can crack carbon tubes. |
| Rear derailleur hanger bolt | 8 to 10 Nm | Holds the derailleur to the hanger. Overtightening can bend or crack the hanger. |
| Pedal spindle (into crank) | 35 Nm | Holds the pedal in the crank. Loose pedals can thread out and damage the crank. |

### Frame and accessories

| Fastener | Typical torque | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Water bottle cage bolts | 4 to 5 Nm on aluminum | Holds the cage on the frame. Carbon frames usually need less. Check the frame spec. |
| Rack or fender mounts | 4 to 6 Nm | Holds accessories. Overtightening cracks mounts. |

## Why the values matter

- Too loose: parts slip, rattle, and wear. Brakes and wheels can move under load, which is a safety risk.
- Too tight: threads strip, aluminum deforms, carbon cracks, and bolts stretch. A stretched bolt loses clamping force and can fail later.

## Checking the values

- Confirm the value stamped on the part or in the manufacturer's manual, especially for carbon components and newer standards.
- If no value is listed, use the lower end of the range for the part's material.
- Recheck bolts after the first few rides, especially on new carbon parts, because bolts can settle.

# Torque Wrench Guide for Bikes

## What a torque wrench is for

A torque wrench measures how hard you tighten a fastener. Torque is the twisting force on a bolt, measured in newton metres (Nm) in bike work. Bike parts use thin aluminium, carbon fibre, and small threads, so the correct tightness matters more than on most machines.

Two failure modes drive the need for a torque wrench:

- **Under-tightening** lets parts slip, rattle, or loosen. A stem that turns under load, a crank that works loose, or a wheel that comes out can cause a crash.
- **Over-tightening** stretches or strips threads, crushes or cracks carbon parts, and warps clamps. Carbon frames and bars can fail with no warning after an over-torqued bolt.

A torque wrench lets you hit the value the manufacturer specifies. Feel alone cannot do that reliably.

## Types

- **Click type**: sets a value, clicks when reached. Most common for bikes. Use the range that fits the bolt, usually 2 to 15 Nm for small parts and 20 to 60 Nm for cranks and cassette lockrings.
- **Beam type**: a pointer on a scale. Cheap and accurate, but you must read it at eye level.
- **Digital type**: shows the reading and often beeps at the target. Useful for carbon work.

Use a wrench that covers the target value near the middle of its range for best accuracy. Have click wrenches checked or calibrated on a schedule.

## Common torque values

These are typical ranges. Always use the value printed on the part or in the manufacturer's manual. Carbon parts often specify lower values than the ranges below.

### Cockpit

| Part | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Stem faceplate bolts | 4 to 6 Nm | Clamps the steerer. Too tight can crack the stem or crush a carbon steerer. Too loose lets the stem slip. |
| Handlebar clamp bolts | 5 to 6 Nm | Holds the bar in the stem. Carbon bars often need a specific lower value. |
| Brake or shifter lever clamp | 2 to 5 Nm | Keeps the lever from rotating. Small bolts strip easily. |
| Seatpost clamp | 5 to 7 Nm | Holds the post at the height set. Carbon posts usually need a lower value. |
| Saddle rail clamp | 6 to 8 Nm | Holds the saddle angle and position. |
| Headset top cap bolt | 5 to 8 Nm, per fork | Preloads the headset bearings. Too tight causes binding, too loose causes play. |

### Wheels and brakes

| Part | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Caliper mounting bolts (disc) | 6 to 8 Nm | Keeps the caliper aligned with the rotor. |
| Rotor bolts (six-bolt) | 4 to 6 Nm | Holds the rotor so it does not wobble or come loose. |
| Centerlock lockring | about 40 Nm, per hub | Holds the rotor on the hub. Use the tool for the lockring. |
| Hydraulic hose banjo bolts | 5 to 7 Nm | Seals the fluid line. Too tight can crack the fitting. |
| Thru axle (12 or 15 mm) | 10 to 15 Nm, per hub | Clamps the wheel in the dropouts. Check the hub spec. |
| Quick release | Not torqued | Set by the lever force. Check the closing pressure instead. |

### Drivetrain

| Part | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Crank bolt (Hollowtech or similar) | 35 to 50 Nm, per crank | Holds the crank on the spindle. Loose cranks wear the spindle and can slip. |
| Bottom bracket (threaded) | 35 to 50 Nm | Holds the cups in the frame. Too tight can damage threads. |
| Pedals | 30 to 35 Nm | Holds the pedal in the crank. Left pedal has a reverse thread. |
| Chainring bolts | 8 to 12 Nm | Holds rings to the crank arm. Tighten in a star pattern. |
| Cassette lockring | 30 to 50 Nm | Holds the cassette on the freehub. Loose cassettes click and wear. |
| Rear derailleur hanger bolt | 8 to 10 Nm | Holds the derailleur on the frame. Check the hanger for damage. |
| Derailleur mount bolt | 5 to 6 Nm | Holds the derailleur body. |
| Cable pinch bolt | 4 to 5 Nm | Clamps the cable. Over-tightening frays it. |

### Frame and accessories

| Part | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Water bottle cage bolts | 4 to 5 Nm | Holds the cage without cracking the frame boss. Carbon frames often need less. |
| Rack and fender mounts | 3 to 5 Nm | Small bolts that carry load. Light torque avoids stripping. |

## Practical tips

- Check the part for a torque figure first. Carbon parts especially.
- Work the bolts in a cross or star pattern when a part has several bolts.
- Use a torque wrench on the final tighten. Install with a hex key and then set the value.
- Do not use grease or anti-seize on carbon or on parts whose spec says dry. These lubricants change the torque reading. Use only what the manufacturer specifies.
- Keep the wrench in a clean case and check it on a schedule.

## Caution

These values are general guidance, not a substitute for the part's own specification. If the part has no value printed and you are unsure, ask the manufacturer or a senior mechanic before tightening.

# Torque Wrench Guide for Bicycles

## What a torque wrench is for

A torque wrench measures how hard you tighten a fastener. Bicycle parts are small, often made of aluminum or carbon fiber, and many bolts are very small. Hand tightening by feel is the most common cause of loose parts and broken parts.

Too loose causes slipping, rattling, creaking, wheels or cranks coming off, and brake or drivetrain misalignment. Too tight causes stripped threads, cracked carbon, crushed steerers, warped rotors, and seized parts that are hard to remove later.

A click type torque wrench clicks when it reaches the set value. Stop turning when you hear the click. Do not keep turning past it. Store the wrench at its lowest setting so the internal spring stays relaxed. Have it checked or recalibrated on a regular schedule.

Common sizes are 1/4 inch drive for low torque (stems, clamps, accessories) and 3/8 inch drive for higher torque (cranks, bottom brackets, cassette lockrings). Use a bit that fits the bolt head fully. A worn or loose bit can strip the head.

Units: 1 Nm equals about 8.85 in-lb. Many wrenches read in only one unit, so convert when needed.

## Common torque values

Always check the value printed on the part or in the manufacturer's manual first. These values are typical ranges. Use the lower end when the part is carbon or the manufacturer says so.

| Location | Typical torque | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Stem faceplate bolts (threadless steerer) | 5 to 6 Nm, some models up to 8 Nm | Clamps the steerer. Too tight can crack a carbon steerer or crush an aluminum one. Too loose lets the stem slip. |
| Stem top cap bolt | 2 to 5 Nm | Sets headset preload. Tighten only after the stem bolts are set, so the bearings are not too tight or too loose. |
| Handlebar clamp bolts (stem to bars) | 4 to 6 Nm | Holds the bars. Carbon bars often need 5 Nm or less. |
| Seatpost clamp bolt | 5 to 6 Nm | Holds the post in the frame. Carbon posts and frames often have a lower maximum. |
| Saddle rail clamp bolts | 4 to 6 Nm | Holds the saddle to the post. Loose rails let the saddle tilt or move. |
| Brake lever clamp bolts | 5 to 6 Nm | Holds the lever to the bar. Too loose lets the lever rotate. |
| Brake caliper mounting bolts (rim and disc) | 6 to 8 Nm, flat mount may be higher | Holds the caliper to the frame or fork. Loose calipers cause braking problems. |
| Disc rotor bolts (6 bolt) | 2.5 to 6 Nm, check the rotor | Holds the rotor to the hub. Tighten in a star pattern to keep the rotor flat. Too tight can warp the rotor. |
| Shifter and derailleur cable pinch bolts | 4 to 6 Nm | Holds the cable. Too tight can crush the cable housing or the shifter. |
| Rear derailleur mounting bolt | 8 to 10 Nm | Holds the derailleur to the hanger. Loose bolts cause shifting problems. |
| Derailleur hanger bolt | 8 to 10 Nm | Holds the hanger to the frame. Check the hanger alignment after tightening. |
| Chainring bolts | 8 to 12 Nm | Holds the rings to the crank. Tighten in a star pattern. Loose rings wear the crank and drop the chain. |
| Crank bolt (self extracting or Hollowtech style) | 35 to 50 Nm | Holds the crank to the bottom bracket spindle. Too loose lets the crank come off. Too tight can damage the spindle. |
| Pedals into cranks | 35 to 40 Nm | Holds the pedal in the crank. Use grease on the threads. Pedal threads are reverse on the left pedal, so tighten the left pedal counterclockwise. |
| Bottom bracket (threaded) | 35 to 50 Nm | Holds the cups in the frame. Check the frame standard first. Too tight can crack the shell. |
| Cassette lockring | 30 to 50 Nm, often 40 Nm | Holds the cassette on the freehub body. Too loose lets the cassette move and skip. |
| Thru axle or quick release axle nuts (front) | 10 to 15 Nm | Holds the wheel to the fork. Check the hub label. Quick releases are set by lever force, not torque. |
| Thru axle or axle nuts (rear) | 15 to 20 Nm | Holds the wheel to the frame. Check the hub label. |
| Bottle cage bolts | 1 to 2 Nm | Small bolts in carbon or aluminum frames. Overtightening can crack the frame boss. |
| Rack and fender mounting bolts | 4 to 6 Nm | Holds accessories to the frame. Use less torque on carbon frames. |

## Practical notes

- Use a clean, dry thread unless the manufacturer says to add grease or threadlocker. Grease or threadlocker changes the torque reading, so follow the spec for that condition.
- Use the right order for multi bolt parts. Tighten rotors, chainrings, and caliper bolts in a star or cross pattern, in small steps, then the final value.
- Carbon parts need a torque wrench and the manufacturer value. Do not guess.
- Replace any bolt with a damaged head or stripped threads. Do not reuse a damaged bolt.
- Check torque again after the first few rides on new parts, since the parts can settle.

## Safety

If a value is not known, do not guess. Check the part for a printed value or look up the manufacturer manual. If the frame or part is carbon and the value is unknown, use the lower end of the typical range.

**Cleaning:** Wash the frame with mild soap and water, then dry it fully. Degrease the chain and cassette to remove grit and old lube. Wipe the rims and brake pads clean.

**Lubrication:** When the chain is dry, apply a light lube and wipe off the excess. Grease the seatpost, pedal threads, and exposed bolts to prevent rust.

**Tires:** Inflate the tires to about two thirds of their normal pressure so the rubber does not crack. Lift the wheels off the floor, or check the pressure monthly.

**Where to keep the bike:** Store the bike indoors in a cool, dry spot away from heat. Avoid damp basements and unheated sheds, where rust and mold form.

**Cleaning:** Wash the frame with mild soap and water, then dry it fully. Wipe grit off the drivetrain and chain.

**Lubrication:** Oil the chain lightly, then wipe off the excess so it does not collect dust. Grease the seatpost and pedal threads. Spray cables and brake pivots.

**Storage:** Keep the bike indoors in a dry, cool spot away from heat and direct sun. Hang it or rest it on a stand, and cover it loosely to keep dust off.

# Brake Check Procedure for New Volunteers

Use this procedure before any bike leaves the shop with a brake check. Read the section for the bike's brake type. Rim brakes and disc brakes are checked differently.

If you are unsure what a bike has, look at the brake. A rim brake clamps the wheel rim. A disc brake has a metal rotor bolted to the hub and a caliper straddling it.

## Before you start (both types)

1. Put the bike in a stand, or turn it upside down on a clean surface with the wheels free.
2. Check both wheels. The quick release lever or through axle must be fully closed or tight. Give each wheel a sideways shake. It should not move.
3. Check the brake levers. Squeeze each one. It should feel firm and stop the wheel when pulled.
4. Tell the shop lead before you start if you find anything listed under "Stop and tag the bike" below.

## Rim brakes (caliper or V brakes)

### 1. Brake pads
- Look for the wear indicator groove on each pad. If the groove is gone, replace the pads.
- Replace pads that are cracked, hard, shiny, or contaminated with oil or grease.
- Check that each pad sits flat against the rim with the front edge slightly toed in. The front edge should touch the rim a moment before the back edge.

- Pads worn to the wear limit or contaminated with oil.

# Bike Tour Packing Guide (7 days)

Each item lists the reason it matters.

## 1. Bike and repair kit

- **Bike case or padded bag.** Protects the frame and derailleur on the flight. Airlines often damage bikes that travel unprotected.
- **Tire levers (3).** Remove a tire without pinching a new tube.
- **Spare tubes (2) and a patch kit.** Flat tires are the most common roadside failure.
- **Mini pump or CO2 inflator.** A tube is useless without air.
- **Multitool with hex keys and chain breaker.** Covers most bolt adjustments and chain repairs.
- **Spare quick link and a few chain links.** Repairs a snapped chain in minutes.
- **Spare derailleur hanger, if your bike uses one.** A bent hanger can end the tour. A spare lets you keep riding.
- **Chain lube and a rag.** Dust and rain wear a chain quickly. Lube keeps shifting smooth.
- **Spoke wrench.** Fixes a loose spoke before the wheel goes out of true.
- **Zip ties, duct tape, and a few cable ties.** Makes emergency fixes to racks, bags, and cables.

## 2. Cycling clothing

# Winter Storage Routine

Cleaning
Wipe the frame, fork, and components with a damp cloth and mild dish soap. Degrease the drivetrain with a brush and solvent, rinse off any residue, and dry every part fully. Check the chain and cassette for rust. Clean the rims and brake pads so grit does not sit on them over winter.

Lubrication
Once the drivetrain is clean and dry, apply a fresh coat of chain lube and wipe off the excess. Lubricate the derailleur pivots, cable housing ends, brake and shifter pivots, and the seatpost. Lightly grease the pedal threads and seatpost. Keep lube off the brake rotors and pads.

Tires
Inflate the tires to a moderate pressure, about half the maximum printed on the sidewall, so they keep their shape. Check the sidewalls for cracks. If the bike will sit for several months, hang it off the ground or lower the pressure slightly. Rotate the wheels once midseason if the bike stays unused.

Where to keep the bike
Store the bike indoors in a dry place away from freezing temperatures, direct sunlight, and damp floors. Hang it by the frame or on a stand so the tires stay off the floor. Cover it loosely to keep dust off, and do not lean it against a damp wall.

# Roadside Tube Patch Guide

Read this once before you start. Work slowly. Most failed patches come from rushing the cleaning or the glue step.

## What you need
- Tire levers (2 or 3), or your hands if the tire is loose enough
- Patch kit: patches, sandpaper or a scuffer, rubber cement, and a small tube of glue
- A pump or CO2 inflator
- A small bowl of water or a sense of where the hole is (for finding leaks)

## Step 1: Stop and find the cause
Pull over somewhere safe. Look at the tire for anything still stuck in it: glass, thorns, wire. Remove it with pliers or your fingers. If you skip this, the new tube will go flat again.

## Step 2: Remove the wheel
- Rear wheel: shift into the smallest rear cog, then open the quick release or undo the axle nuts. Lift the chain off the cog if needed, then pull the wheel out.
- Front wheel: open the quick release or undo the axle nuts and lift the wheel out.
- Do not press the brake lever while the wheel is out of the frame.

## Step 3: Deflate and pull one bead off the rim
- Push the valve core (the small pin in the valve tip) to let out any remaining air.
- Press the tire bead (the tire edge) into the center of the rim all the way around. This gives you slack.
- Work one side of the tire off the rim with your hands. If it is tight, use a tire lever about 10 cm from the valve and pry the bead up. Do not use a lever near the valve.
- Hook the second lever under the bead and pry it over the rim. Keep the lever's hook on a spoke so it cannot slip off.

## Step 4: Remove the tube
- Pull the valve out of the rim hole first, then pull the tube out of the tire.
- Keep the tire in place on the rim with one bead still on.

## Step 5: Find the hole
- Pump the tube with a little air. Hold it near your cheek or ear and listen for a hiss, or feel for air on your skin.
- If you cannot hear it, dunk small sections in water and watch for bubbles.
- Mark the spot with a pen or chalk.
- Check the tire inside for the sharp thing that caused the flat. Run your fingers slowly around the inside.

## Step 6: Prepare the patch area
- Dry the tube completely.
- Scuff a patch-sized area around the hole with sandpaper, about 2 cm across. The surface should look rough and dull.
- Wipe off the dust. Do not touch the scuffed area with your fingers.

## Step 7: Apply glue
- Spread a thin, even layer of rubber cement over the scuffed area. Use a little more than the patch size.
- Let it dry until it is tacky and no longer wet. This usually takes 1 to 3 minutes. Do not blow on it.

## Step 8: Apply the patch
- Peel the foil backing off the patch.
- Place the patch on the glue, centered over the hole.
- Press firmly with your thumb for about 30 seconds. Press from the middle outward to push air out.
- Leave the plastic film on if the patch has one, unless the instructions say to remove it.

## Step 9: Put the tube back in
- Dust the tube lightly with talc or chalk if you have it. This stops the tube from sticking to the tire.
- Put a little air in the tube so it takes shape.
- Insert the valve into the rim hole first.
- Tuck the tube into the tire evenly. Make sure it is not twisted or pinched between the tire and the rim.

## Step 10: Reseat the tire
- Push the tire bead back onto the rim with your hands, starting at the valve and working both ways.
- For the last section, use your thumbs. Do not use a tire lever here, because it can pinch the tube.
- Check that the tube is not showing along the rim edge on either side.

## Step 11: Inflate carefully
- Inflate to about half the pressure printed on the tire sidewall.
- Look and feel around the rim to check the tube is seated evenly.
- Then inflate to full pressure.
- Keep the wheel from spinning and rubbing the brake until it is seated.

## Step 12: Refit the wheel
- Put the wheel back in the frame. Make sure it is centered between the fork or stays.
- Rear wheel: place the chain back on the smallest cog if it came off.
- Close the quick release with the lever on the drive side (for a rear wheel, the non-chain side), or tighten the axle nuts evenly.
- Spin the wheel and check that it does not rub the brake pads or frame.

## Step 13: Final check
- Squeeze the brake levers and check they stop the wheel.
- Check the tire is not bulging at any spot.
- Ride slowly for a few meters, then check the tire pressure again.

## Tips
- Carry a spare tube. It is faster than patching at the roadside.
- If the tube has a large tear or more than one hole, replace it.
- Patch at home later if you want, and keep the patched tube as a spare.

- Let it dry until it is tacky and no longer wet. This usually takes 1 to 3 minutes. Do not blow on it.

## Step 8: Apply the patch
- Peel the foil backing off the patch.
- Place the patch on the glue, centered over the hole.
- Press firmly with your thumb for about 30 seconds. Press from the middle outward to push air out.
- Leave the plastic film on if the patch has one, unless the instructions say to remove it.

## Step 9: Put the tube back in
- Dust the tube lightly with talc or chalk if you have it. This stops the tube from sticking to the tire.
- Put a little air in the tube so it takes shape.
- Insert the valve into the rim hole first.
- Tuck the tube into the tire evenly. Make sure it is not twisted or pinched between the tire and the rim.

## Step 10: Reseat the tire
- Push the tire bead back onto the rim with your hands, starting at the valve and working both ways.
- For the last section, use your thumbs. Do not use a tire lever here, because it can pinch the tube.
- Check that the tube is not showing along the rim edge on either side.

## Step 11: Inflate carefully
- Inflate to about half the pressure printed on the tire sidewall.
- Look and feel around the rim to check the tube is seated evenly.
- Then inflate to full pressure.
- Keep the wheel from spinning and rubbing the brake until it is seated.

## Step 12: Refit the wheel
- Put the wheel back in the frame. Make sure it is centered between the fork or stays.
- Rear wheel: place the chain back on the smallest cog if it came off.
- Close the quick release with the lever on the drive side (for a rear wheel, the non-chain side), or tighten the axle nuts evenly.
- Spin the wheel and check that it does not rub the brake pads or frame.

## Step 13: Final check
- Squeeze the brake levers and check they stop the wheel.
- Check the tire is not bulging at any spot.
- Ride slowly for a few meters, then check the tire pressure again.

## Tips
- Carry a spare tube. It is faster than patching at the roadside.
- If the tube has a large tear or more than one hole, replace it.
- Patch at home later if you want, and keep the patched tube as a spare.

# Week-Long Bike Tour Packing Guide

This guide lists what to pack for a seven-day bike tour, with the reason for each item. It assumes you fly with a bike and camp or stay in lodging along the route.

## 1. Bike and travel case

- Bike box or hard case. Airlines damage soft bags less often in hard cases, and a box keeps the frame protected.
- Pedals, handlebar turned, seat post lowered, wheels off as needed. Removing parts shrinks the box and protects derailleurs.
- Tools to take the bike apart and reassemble: multi-tool, pedal wrench, hex keys, tire levers.
- Spare derailleur hanger. A bent hanger can end a tour, and this part is often unavailable on the road.
- Paper or phone copy of the airline bike policy and fees. Airlines differ on size and cost.

## 2. Repair kit (carry on the bike or in a handlebar bag)

- Two spare tubes that match your wheel size and valve type. Presta and Schrader valves are not interchangeable without an adapter.
- Patch kit and glue. Patches cover small holes when a tube is still usable.
- Tire levers, two or three. Plastic levers avoid pinching the tube.
- Mini pump or CO2 inflator with spare cartridges. Confirm CO2 cartridges are allowed on your flight before you pack them.
- Chain tool and a quick link. Chains break on tours more often than people expect.
- Spoke wrench sized to your wheels.
- Zip ties and a few strips of duct tape wrapped around a pencil or stick. These fix brackets, racks, and bags.
- Spare brake pads and a spare cable for the brake type you run.
- Spare bulb or light batteries and a charger.

## 3. Cycling clothing

- Three to four padded cycling shorts. Padding wears out with use, and washing sometimes takes a full day in a hostel.
- Three to four jerseys or technical shirts. Synthetic or wool fabrics dry overnight.
- One long-sleeve base layer for cool mornings or descents.
- Lightweight rain jacket with a hood. Rain on a long descent makes the cold worse than the rain.
- Arm warmers or a light wind vest. These add warmth without much bulk.
- Gloves, one pair of full-finger for cool days and fingerless for warm days.
- Thin wool or synthetic socks, three to four pairs. Cotton stays wet and causes blisters.
- Cycling cap or buff for sun and wind under the helmet.
- Sunglasses with a spare lens or a case.

## 4. Off-bike clothing

- Two lightweight shirts and one pair of shorts or pants for evenings. Lodging and restaurants often expect non-cycling clothes.
- One warm layer such as a fleece or light down jacket. Evenings in higher or coastal areas can drop well below daytime temperatures.
- Sleepwear, one set.
- Underwear, enough for seven days or a plan to wash.
- Sandals or light shoes for showers and walking. Cycling shoes are hard to walk in and hard on hostel floors.

## 5. Footwear

- Cycling shoes you have already ridden in for at least 300 kilometers. A new pair can cause hot spots by day three.
- Clipless pedal cleats, if your pedals use them, and spare cleat bolts.
- Pedal platforms are an alternative if you use flat pedals.

## 6. Sleeping and camping (if you camp)

- Tent or hammock with stakes and a pole repair sleeve.
- Sleeping bag rated for the lowest expected night temperature, plus a few degrees margin.
- Sleeping pad. Ground cold steals sleep quickly.
- Pillow or stuff sack filled with clothes to save space.
- Headlamp with spare batteries.

## 7. Toiletries and health

- Sunscreen, SPF 30 or higher, and lip balm with SPF.
- Chamois cream to reduce saddle chafing.
- Anti-chafe balm or powder for skin contact points.
- Pain reliever, anti-diarrheal, and any prescription medicine in its original container. Keep prescriptions in the carry-on bag.
- Bandages, antiseptic wipes, blister pads, and tape.
- Basic toiletries in travel sizes. Liquids over the allowed size belong in checked luggage.
- Hand sanitizer and a small towel.
- Insect repellent if the route crosses wet or wooded areas.

## 8. Navigation, electronics, and documents

- Phone with offline maps downloaded before the flight. Maps will not load on a dead signal.
- Cycling computer or GPS unit, with the route file loaded.
- Mount for the phone or computer, and a spare charging cable.
- Power bank rated for at least 10,000 mAh. Carry it in the cabin, since airlines restrict lithium batteries in checked bags.
- Wall charger and a plug adapter for the destination country.
- Headphones and a small speaker if you want them.
- Passport, ID, insurance card, bike insurance paperwork, and emergency contacts. Store copies in a separate place.
- Cash in local currency and one or two cards. Some rural areas accept no card.
- Printed route cue sheet or saved route file. Battery and signal failures happen.

## 9. Bags and carry

- Frame bag or top tube bag for tools, snacks, and the phone.
- Handlebar bag for items you need during the day, such as the rain jacket and sunscreen.
- Saddle bag or seat pack for the repair kit.
- Panniers, front and rear, with waterproof liners. Keep weight low and balanced, and fill the rear bags first.
- Dry bags for sleeping gear and electronics. Rain can soak through panniers.
- Small day pack for sightseeing off the bike.

## 10. Food and water

- Two water bottles or a hydration bladder. A second bottle doubles the water you can carry between towns.
- Electrolyte tablets or powder for hot days.
- Energy bars, nuts, or dried fruit for emergencies.
- A water filter or purification tablets if the route uses natural water sources.

## 11. Carry-on items to keep with you

- Passport and tickets.
- Medicine and a copy of the prescription.
- Phone, power bank, and charging cable.
- One change of clothes and toiletries in case checked luggage is delayed.
- The bike tools needed for reassembly at the destination, in case the bike case arrives without them.

## 12. Pre-departure checks

- Test-ride the bike with the loaded panniers before the trip.
- Check brake pads, tire wear, and chain stretch.
- Confirm the bike box fits the airline size limit.
- Confirm the lodging and campsite bookings for each night.
- Share your route and daily plan with someone at home.
- Charge all devices and bring the chargers.

## Weight and space guide

Keep the loaded bike and bags under about 15 percent of your body weight when you can. Heavier loads make hills harder and raise the risk of rack or wheel failure.

- Clipless pedal cleats, if your pedals use them, and spare cleat bolts.
- Pedal platforms are an alternative if you use flat pedals.

## 6. Sleeping and camping (if you camp)

- Tent or hammock with stakes and a pole repair sleeve.
- Sleeping bag rated for the lowest expected night temperature, plus a few degrees margin.
- Sleeping pad. Ground cold steals sleep quickly.
- Pillow or stuff sack filled with clothes to save space.
- Headlamp with spare batteries.

## 7. Toiletries and health

- Sunscreen, SPF 30 or higher, and lip balm with SPF.
- Chamois cream to reduce saddle chafing.
- Anti-chafe balm or powder for skin contact points.
- Pain reliever, anti-diarrheal, and any prescription medicine in its original container. Keep prescriptions in the carry-on bag.
- Bandages, antiseptic wipes, blister pads, and tape.
- Basic toiletries in travel sizes. Liquids over the allowed size belong in checked luggage.
- Hand sanitizer and a small towel.
- Insect repellent if the route crosses wet or wooded areas.

## 8. Navigation, electronics, and documents

- Phone with offline maps downloaded before the flight. Maps will not load on a dead signal.
- Cycling computer or GPS unit, with the route file loaded.
- Mount for the phone or computer, and a spare charging cable.
- Power bank rated for at least 10,000 mAh. Carry it in the cabin, since airlines restrict lithium batteries in checked bags.
- Wall charger and a plug adapter for the destination country.
- Headphones and a small speaker if you want them.
- Passport, ID, insurance card, bike insurance paperwork, and emergency contacts. Store copies in a separate place.
- Cash in local currency and one or two cards. Some rural areas accept no card.
- Printed route cue sheet or saved route file. Battery and signal failures happen.

## 9. Bags and carry

- Frame bag or top tube bag for tools, snacks, and the phone.
- Handlebar bag for items you need during the day, such as the rain jacket and sunscreen.
- Saddle bag or seat pack for the repair kit.
- Panniers, front and rear, with waterproof liners. Keep weight low and balanced, and fill the rear bags first.
- Dry bags for sleeping gear and electronics. Rain can soak through panniers.
- Small day pack for sightseeing off the bike.

## 10. Food and water

- Two water bottles or a hydration bladder. A second bottle doubles the water you can carry between towns.
- Electrolyte tablets or powder for hot days.
- Energy bars, nuts, or dried fruit for emergencies.
- A water filter or purification tablets if the route uses natural water sources.

## 11. Carry-on items to keep with you

- Passport and tickets.
- Medicine and a copy of the prescription.
- Phone, power bank, and charging cable.
- One change of clothes and toiletries in case checked luggage is delayed.
- The bike tools needed for reassembly at the destination, in case the bike case arrives without them.

## 12. Pre-departure checks

- Test-ride the bike with the loaded panniers before the trip.
- Check brake pads, tire wear, and chain stretch.
- Confirm the bike box fits the airline size limit.
- Confirm the lodging and campsite bookings for each night.
- Share your route and daily plan with someone at home.
- Charge all devices and bring the chargers.

## Weight and space guide

Keep the loaded bike and bags under about 15 percent of your body weight when you can. Heavier loads make hills harder and raise the risk of rack or wheel failure.

# Torque Wrenches and Bike Torque Values

## What a torque wrench is for

A torque wrench measures how hard you tighten a fastener. Bike bolts are small, and many are made of aluminum or carbon fiber. Tighten too little and parts can loosen, rattle, or come off while riding. Tighten too much and threads can strip, aluminum can deform, carbon can crack, and bolts can snap.

Torque is a force applied at a distance, measured in newton meters (Nm) in most bike specifications. Feel alone is not reliable. Two people can tighten the same bolt to very different levels.

A click type torque wrench clicks when the set value is reached. A beam type shows the value on a scale. A digital wrench shows the reading on a screen. Click type wrenches are the most common in bike shops. Store them at the lowest setting, because a wrench left at high tension loses calibration over time.

Parts often have a maximum torque printed on them. Always check the manufacturer spec for the exact part. The values below are typical ranges for common bikes. They do not replace the printed spec.

## Common torque values

Values are typical ranges in Nm. Use the lower end for carbon parts and small bolts.

### Cockpit

- Stem faceplate bolts: 5 to 6 Nm. Clamps the handlebar. Too loose lets the bar rotate. Too tight can crush the bar.
- Stem steerer expander bolt (top cap): 4 to 6 Nm. Expands the steerer plug to lock the stem to the fork. Loose stems can slip or rattle.
- Handlebar clamp bolts: about 5 Nm. Holds the bar in place. Carbon bars often need 5 Nm or less.
- Brake lever clamp: 4 to 5 Nm. Keeps lever angle set. Too tight can crack carbon bars.
- Shifter clamp: 2 to 4 Nm. Holds the shifter. Too tight can damage the bar or shifter.

### Seatpost and saddle

- Seatpost clamp: 5 to 6 Nm. Holds the seatpost. Loose posts slip under load. Carbon posts need extra care.
- Saddle rail clamp (seat binder): 5 to 7 Nm. Holds saddle rails in the post head. Too tight can crack rails or the clamp.

### Brakes

- Rim brake caliper mount: 6 to 8 Nm. Keeps the caliper aligned and stops it from moving under braking.
- Disc brake caliper mount: 6 to 8 Nm. Keeps the caliper aligned over the rotor. Loose mounts cause rubbing or lost braking power.
- Disc rotor bolts (six bolt pattern): about 2.5 to 6 Nm. Holds the rotor. Values vary by brand, so check the spec. Too tight can warp the rotor.
- Disc rotor center lock: about 40 Nm. Large lockring that secures the rotor on splined hubs. Follow the rotor maker spec.
- Hydraulic hose banjo bolt: 5 to 8 Nm. Seals the fluid line. Use new crush washers each time the banjo is undone. Loose fittings leak fluid.

### Drivetrain

- Pedals into crank: 35 to 40 Nm. Pedal threads are soft. Too loose lets a pedal back out. Too tight damages crank threads. Apply grease first if the pedal spec allows.
- Crank arm bolt (Hollowtech or similar): 35 to 50 Nm. Holds the crank onto the spindle. Loose cranks can damage the bottom bracket and crank.
- Bottom bracket cups or lockring: 35 to 50 Nm. Holds the bottom bracket in the frame. Check the cup type, since threaded and press fit designs differ.
- Chainring bolts: 8 to 12 Nm. Holds rings onto the crank spider. Loose rings wear and can drop the chain.
- Cassette lockring: 30 to 50 Nm. Holds the cassette on the freehub body. Loose cassettes can spin and damage the hub.
- Rear derailleur hanger bolt: 8 to 10 Nm. Holds the derailleur to the hanger. Loose derailleurs shift poorly.
- Front derailleur clamp: 5 to 7 Nm. Holds the front derailleur on the seat tube. Too tight can crack carbon frames.

### Wheels and frame

- Thru axle, front: about 10 to 15 Nm. Holds the front wheel in the fork. Check the axle maker spec.
- Thru axle, rear: about 15 to 20 Nm. Holds the rear wheel in the frame. Check the axle maker spec.
- Solid axle nuts: 15 to 20 Nm. Holds the wheel on the axle. Quick releases are set by hand, not with a torque wrench.
- Water bottle cage bolts: 4 to 5 Nm. Holds the cage. Carbon frames often need less.
- Rack and fender bolts: 4 to 5 Nm. Holds accessories. Overtightening strips threads in frame bosses.

## Practical tips

- Check the printed spec on the part first. If unsure, use the lower value and recheck.
- Clean threads and grease only where the spec allows. Some specs assume dry threads, and grease changes the torque reading.
- Do final tightening with the torque wrench. On multi bolt parts such as stems and rotors, tighten in a cross pattern.
- Use a torque wrench on every bolt of a carbon part.
- Replace crush washers and single use bolts when the manufacturer says to.
- Store the wrench at its lowest setting.

## Limits

These numbers are general ranges for common bikes. Brands and models differ, and some specs are narrow. Use the printed spec on the part or the manufacturer manual when it is available.

# Roadside Tube Patch Guide

This guide walks through fixing a flat tube on the road. Read each step once before you start.

## What you need

1. A spare tube that matches the wheel size, such as 700c, if you have one.
2. Two or three tire levers.
3. A hand pump or CO2 inflator.
4. A tube patch kit, with patches, rubber cement, and sandpaper or a scuffer.
5. A small piece of tire or a dollar bill to use as a boot for large cuts in the tire.
6. Any tool that loosens the wheel, usually a 15 mm wrench or a hex key for thru axles.

## Step 1: Stop and get safe

Move the bike off the traffic lane. Lay it on its non drive side, or lean it against something solid.

## Step 2: Open the brake and remove the wheel

For a quick release lever, open the lever fully and turn the nut on the other side counterclockwise until the wheel slides out.

For axle nuts, loosen both nuts evenly.

For the rear wheel, shift the chain to the smallest cog at the back. Pull the rear derailleur backward and lift the wheel out of the frame. Keep the chain on the smallest cog while the wheel is out.

## Step 3: Let out the remaining air

Press the valve pin to release any air still in the tube. For a Presta valve, unscrew the top nut first, then press the pin.

## Step 4: Pull one side of the tire off the rim

Push the tire bead, which is the stiff edge of the tire, toward the center of the rim near the valve. This gives you slack.

Hook the first tire lever under the bead, about 10 cm from the valve. Pry it up and over the rim edge.

Hook the second lever under the bead a hand width away, and pry it over the rim. Do not use a third lever yet.

If needed, slide the second lever along the rim, one spoke at a time, to lift the bead off the rim.

## Step 5: Remove the tube

Pull the valve stem out of the rim hole first. Then pull the rest of the tube out from under the tire.

## Step 6: Find the cause and the hole

Slightly inflate the tube so it is round. Listen for escaping air, or run wet fingers slowly along the tube. Bubbles or a hiss show the hole. Mark the spot with a pen or a piece of tape.

Inspect the inside of the tire by running your fingers slowly around it. Remove any glass, thorns, or wire you find. If you do not remove the cause, the new tube will go flat too.

If the tire has a cut larger than about 1 cm, place a folded bill or a piece of tire inside the tire over the cut. This stops the tube from bulging into the cut.

If the tube has two small holes side by side, it is likely a pinch flat from hitting a curb or pothole at low pressure. Patch both holes or replace the tube.

## Step 7: Patch the tube

If you are patching instead of replacing the tube, follow the kit steps.

1. Let the tube air out.
2. Scuff the area around the hole with sandpaper, about twice the patch size.
3. Apply a thin layer of rubber cement and let it dry until it feels tacky, about 1 to 2 minutes.
4. Remove the backing from the patch and press it firmly over the hole.
5. Press hard for about 30 seconds.

Patches need time to bond. If the patch lifts, the glue was not dry enough or the surface was not scuffed.

Roadside, replacing the tube is faster and more reliable. Patching is better at home.

## Step 8: Put the tube back in

Add a small amount of air so the tube keeps its shape. Do not add much air.

Start with the valve. Push the valve stem through its hole in the rim first.

Tuck the tube inside the tire, starting at the valve and working both ways. Make sure the tube is not twisted and is not caught between the tire and the rim.

## Step 9: Seat the tire bead on the rim

Push the tire bead back on the rim with your hands, starting opposite the valve and working toward the valve. Push the last section near the valve with both thumbs.

If the last section is hard to push on, use a tire lever very carefully. Be careful not to pinch the tube under the lever.

Run your fingers around both sides of the tire to check the bead sits evenly in the rim.

## Step 10: Inflate the tire

Add air with a hand pump or a CO2 inflator. Stop at about 30 psi to check that the bead seats evenly on both sides. A bulge or uneven line means the tire is not seated, and you should deflate and fix it.

Then inflate to the pressure printed on the tire sidewall. The usual range is 80 to 130 psi for road tires, so check the number on your tire.

## Step 11: Put the wheel back on

For the rear wheel, place the wheel into the dropouts. Put the chain on the smallest cog. Pull the derailleur back as you set the axle in place.

For the front wheel, place the axle into the dropouts with the brake pads on either side of the rim.

Tighten the quick release: close the lever firmly with your palm, so it leaves a mark on your hand. For axle nuts, tighten both evenly.

Reconnect the brake and close it.

## Step 12: Check before riding

Spin the wheel by hand. It should turn freely without rubbing the brake or the frame.

Squeeze the brake and check it stops the wheel.

Give the wheel a firm shake side to side. It should not move in the dropouts.

Ride slowly for the first minute, and watch the tire for any bulge or wobble.

## Tips

Carry a spare tube and tire levers on every ride. A spare tube fixes a flat in about 10 minutes.

Pump before each ride to the pressure printed on the sidewall. Low pressure makes pinch flats more likely.

# Roadside Tube Patch Guide

This guide walks through fixing a flat tube on the road. Read each step once before you start.

## What you need

1. A spare tube that matches the wheel size, such as 700c, if you have one.
2. Two or three tire levers.
3. A hand pump or CO2 inflator.
4. A tube patch kit, with patches, rubber cement, and sandpaper or a scuffer.
5. A small piece of tire or a dollar bill to use as a boot for large cuts in the tire.
6. Any tool that loosens the wheel, usually a 15 mm wrench or a hex key for thru axles.

## Step 1: Stop and get safe

Move the bike off the traffic lane. Lay it on its non drive side, or lean it against something solid.

## Step 2: Open the brake and remove the wheel

For a quick release lever, open the lever fully and turn the nut on the other side counterclockwise until the wheel slides out.

For axle nuts, loosen both nuts evenly.

For the rear wheel, shift the chain to the smallest cog at the back. Pull the rear derailleur backward and lift the wheel out of the frame. Keep the chain on the smallest cog while the wheel is out.

## Step 3: Let out the remaining air

Press the valve pin to release any air still in the tube. For a Presta valve, unscrew the top nut first, then press the pin.

## Step 4: Pull one side of the tire off the rim

Push the tire bead, which is the stiff edge of the tire, toward the center of the rim near the valve. This gives you slack.

Hook the first tire lever under the bead, about 10 cm from the valve. Pry it up and over the rim edge.

Hook the second lever under the bead a hand width away, and pry it over the rim. Do not use a third lever yet.

If needed, slide the second lever along the rim, one spoke at a time, to lift the bead off the rim.

## Step 5: Remove the tube

Pull the valve stem out of the rim hole first. Then pull the rest of the tube out from under the tire.

## Step 6: Find the cause and the hole

Slightly inflate the tube so it is round. Listen for escaping air, or run wet fingers slowly along the tube. Bubbles or a hiss show the hole. Mark the spot with a pen or a piece of tape.

Inspect the inside of the tire by running your fingers slowly around it. Remove any glass, thorns, or wire you find. If you do not remove the cause, the new tube will go flat too.

If the tire has a cut larger than about 1 cm, place a folded bill or a piece of tire inside the tire over the cut. This stops the tube from bulging into the cut.

If the tube has two small holes side by side, it is likely a pinch flat from hitting a curb or pothole at low pressure. Patch both holes or replace the tube.

## Step 7: Patch the tube

If you are patching instead of replacing the tube, follow the kit steps.

1. Let the tube air out.
2. Scuff the area around the hole with sandpaper, about twice the patch size.
3. Apply a thin layer of rubber cement and let it dry until it feels tacky, about 1 to 2 minutes.
4. Remove the backing from the patch and press it firmly over the hole.
5. Press hard for about 30 seconds.

Patches need time to bond. If the patch lifts, the glue was not dry enough or the surface was not scuffed.

Roadside, replacing the tube is faster and more reliable. Patching is better at home.

## Step 8: Put the tube back in

Add a small amount of air so the tube keeps its shape. Do not add much air.

Start with the valve. Push the valve stem through its hole in the rim first.

Tuck the tube inside the tire, starting at the valve and working both ways. Make sure the tube is not twisted and is not caught between the tire and the rim.

## Step 9: Seat the tire bead on the rim

Push the tire bead back on the rim with your hands, starting opposite the valve and working toward the valve. Push the last section near the valve with both thumbs.

If the last section is hard to push on, use a tire lever very carefully. Be careful not to pinch the tube under the lever.

Run your fingers around both sides of the tire to check the bead sits evenly in the rim.

## Step 10: Inflate the tire

Add air with a hand pump or a CO2 inflator. Stop at about 30 psi to check that the bead seats evenly on both sides. A bulge or uneven line means the tire is not seated, and you should deflate and fix it.

Then inflate to the pressure printed on the tire sidewall. The usual range is 80 to 130 psi for road tires, so check the number on your tire.

## Step 11: Put the wheel back on

For the rear wheel, place the wheel into the dropouts. Put the chain on the smallest cog. Pull the derailleur back as you set the axle in place.

For the front wheel, place the axle into the dropouts with the brake pads on either side of the rim.

Tighten the quick release: close the lever firmly with your palm, so it leaves a mark on your hand. For axle nuts, tighten both evenly.

Reconnect the brake and close it.

## Step 12: Check before riding

Spin the wheel by hand. It should turn freely without rubbing the brake or the frame.

Squeeze the brake and check it stops the wheel.

Give the wheel a firm shake side to side. It should not move in the dropouts.

Ride slowly for the first minute, and watch the tire for any bulge or wobble.

## Tips

Carry a spare tube and tire levers on every ride. A spare tube fixes a flat in about 10 minutes.

Pump before each ride to the pressure printed on the sidewall. Low pressure makes pinch flats more likely.
